I think hon. members feel that a great deal of public business has been transacted this week, in a manner that did not slight the consideration it was proper to give to that business. I am sure that hon. members are anxious to have due consideration given i.o the remaining public business, and that it be dealt with as expeditiously as may be consistent with their responsibility to see that it receives proper consideration.
I imagine that it will be much easier this afternoon for hon. members to give unanimous consent to adjournment at six o'clock if they feel at that time that the progress made during the week has been continued during the day. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuarl S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: UNLAWFUL ACTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is desirable I should make a statement with regard to the latest developments in the matter of the Doukho-bor situation in British Columbia.
Following a further blasting of a section of the Canadian Pacific railway in west Kootenay, British Columbia, Commissioner S. T. Wood, of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, received a telegram from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer in command in British Columbia relaying a request from Commissioner Shirras, British Columbia provincial police, for ten experienced investigators to proceed at once to assist his force in west Kootenay, as he considered the situation serious, and C.P.R. train crews have threatened to discontinue operating trains unless police protection is provided. Furthermore, a request from the provincial government for assistance to this force was to be made officially to me as Minister of Justice within the next day or so.
Commissioner Wood thereupon took the responsibility, in which he has my complete approval, of ordering ten experienced investigators from the prairies and from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel in British Columbia to report without delay to the provincial commissioner at Nelson, B.C. The copy of the instructions of Commissioner Wood to the officer commanding in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police office in Vancouver is as follows:
Officer commanding, R.C.M.P., Vancouver, B.C.- Retel second instant, officers commanding Edmonton. Regina and Winnipeg have been instructed to detail three experienced detachment men respectively to proceed at once to Nelson to operate under the commissioner of the British Columbia police in connection with Doukhobor depredations. They will advise you time of arrival. Please expedite official request from the British Columbia government to our minister for assistance of this force on the understanding that the British Columbia government will pay all expenses. You are to detail one experienced investigator to report to Nelson to British Columbia police.
S. T. Wood
The significance of the stipulation that the British Columbia government should pay all expenses is not so much the amount of the money involved as the continued assertion upon our part of a disclaimer of responsibility. We have neither legal authority nor legal responsibility, and we wish, while

extending the fullest possible co-operation, to have it remain clear that we are assuming no responsibility in a situation in which we have not been involved, even in the matter of extending co-operation, unless it has assumed critical proportions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY

speakeroldname: Hon. Colin Gibson (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 219, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not set myself up

as an expert on gold, but there are one or two aspects of this bill on which I wish to comment briefly.
In effect the bill proposes to continue the subsidizing by the federal treasury of certain gold mines. When the original act was introduced some months ago it received widespread support in the house. In some cases the support was reluctant, but most members agreed with it. The purpose of the original measure was definitely and clearly set out. I should like to quote from the report of the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, published by the Department of Mines and Resources. On page 7 I find the following:
It was designed primarily to assist the high-cost or marginal mines to continue in operation . . .
I ask hon. members to note that it was designed to assist high-cost or marginal mines. I remember the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) speaking in the debate along the same lines. At page 2702 of Hansard of April 6, 1948, he said:
It-
The bonus.
-should enable many mines to avoid closing down . . .
That statement was certainly clear, and the objective of the legislation was specifically stated to be the subsidizing of low-grade mines.
I must say that with that objective I agreed in principle. I thought it was sound then, and I think it is sound today, for the government to give such aid to low-grade mines. But while we are looking at these amendments to the act I think we should analyse the effectiveness of the legislation to date. Have only low-grade mines been subsidized? On the surface at least it would appear that others received assistance also.	From April of
last year to August 31 of this year the taxpayers of Canada have subsidized the gold mines to the extent of about $12,500,000. A fair percentage of this money went to marginal mines, and with that no one will quarrel. United States dollars have been earned; men have been employed; communities have been helped. But at the same time, under this legislation several million dollars apparently have gone to mines that are anything but low-grade. Subsidies have been granted to companies that are among the wealthiest in this country. We find that money has been paid to some corporations which had substantial profits in the past year, and which have paid out dividends in some cases amounting to millions of dollars. When this legislation was passed originally I do not think most hon. members had any idea that this would happen; certainly I did not.
Gold Mining
To give one or two illustrations, take McIntyre Porcupine Mines. On March 31 this company had net current assets of more than $21,600,000. In the last fiscal year it earned net profits of $2,425,000 and paid dividends of $2,405,000; yet the federal treasury gave it a subsidy of $386,000. In view of the robust financial position of this company, I ask the minister how he can justify the payment of such a huge subsidy from the federal treasury.
Then take Hollinger Consolidated Gold Mines. Its assets in the last fiscal year were $7,775,000; its net current assets were almost $2,800,000; it had a net profit of $1,110,000 and paid dividends of $1,109,000; yet the government subsidized it to the extent of $886,000. Dome Mines last year earned over $2,114,000, paid dividends of $1,947,000, had total assests of $16,735,000; yet the taxpayers of Canada subsidized it to the extent of $257,000. Teck-Hughes Gold Mines had net current assets of $1,232,000 and total assets of $9,000,000. Last year it paid out in dividends to its shareholders $721,000; yet it received subsidies amounting to $100,000.
I could go on and give numerous other examples. The point I wish to make is that under this legislation a good many needy gold mines have been assisted, but at the same time some extremely wealthy companies have been given subsidies which so far as I can see were not justified by their financial position. A good many companies which by no stretch of the imagination could be said to have needed that assistance were given it.
On September 19 of this year the government devalued the Canadian dollar. In effect that meant the price of gold went up from $35 to $38.50. Surely that was a final reason why the government should have immediately discontinued subsidies to these wealthy corporations. Certainly the companies themselves have been amazed at the generosity of the government, because according to newspaper reports they thought that when the dollar was devalued the assistance would either be decreased or cut out altogether. I believe they treat this subsidy as a sort of windfall, and are genuinely surprised that it has been continued.
My point is that special assistance to marginal gold mines in Canada is one thing, but assistance to wealthy corporations is quite another. I believe it should be discontinued. I find this policy of subsidizing these wealthy companies all the stranger in view of the past attitude of the government toward ordinary subsidies. I have sat in this house for some years now and have heard most of the cabinet ministers, not once but a

Gold Mining
dozen times, say they are opposed to the principle of peacetime subsidies. For instance, as far back as April 21, 1947 the former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, said, as reported at page 2252 of Hansard:
I think the general view of the government is that we should withdraw from subsidies as far as possible and as soon as possible . . .
There was the case of the milk subsidy, and we have seen the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and others consistently oppose housing subsidies. Time and again the government has opposed subsidies which might have brought down the cost of living. Therefore I find it strange that the bill now before us should propose to subsidize companies which, in my opinion at least, do not seem to need that assistance. I do not see any consistency in this kind of policy. I know some of my Liberal friends would resent it, and perhaps with justification, if I were to say this legislation was discriminatory, or that it was legislation for a privileged group; but if the bill passes in its present form, that is exactly what it will be.
I repeat that so far as this group is concerned we do not oppose subsidies to marginal mines. However, we likewise believe that subsidies to other than marginal mines should be immediately discontinued.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot let the statements just made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) pass without saying a few words on this subject. It seems strange to me that the party to which the hon. member belongs should be at times unfair and antagonistic to gold mining. They do not seem to realize what it means to our whole Canadian economy, not only to northern Canada but to every province of the confederation. The gold mining industry of this country does not want any handout. The hon. member apparently has forgotten that the prices of all other metals, precious or otherwise, have gone up since the beginning of the war. He will not deny that the prices of nickel, copper, steel, lead, zinc, aluminum and all other metals have increased greatly, while the price of gold has been fixed by the United States treasury at $35 an ounce and has not been changed for a good many years. Apparently the hon. member has not read the explanatory note to this bill, from which I should like to read a few lines:
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act provides for payments to gold mines to assist them in defraying part of their post-war increase in cost of production during the designated years 1948, 1949 and 1950.
It is true that this legislation has helped the marginal mines, but it was also meant to help gold mining in general. Coming as

I do from northern Ontario, I would not be in favour of subsidizing mines where the cost of production is too high, or in which the ore would not be exploitable or the ores of too low a grade. At the same time the hon. member cannot deny that the cost of producing gold, the same as any other metal, has increased by at least seventy-five per cent. The cost of labour has increased; the cost of material has gone up, but the price of gold has remained static. If today the mines were receiving $10 an ounce more for their gold, there would be no need for a measure of this kind.
I remember when the Canadian dollar was brought to par a few years ago. I received many telephone calls from companies in my district, for instance from the Spruce Falls newsprint mill at Kapuskasing, the Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company, and others, telling me that they were going to be hurt by that action. I said they would not, because the price of newsprint, of sulphite, of pulpwood and so on was flexible and was not fixed, while the price of gold was in an entirely different position.
I want to compliment this administration because they have understood the situation in connection with gold mining. Personally I am against subsidies, because I believe they camouflage both the real cost of living and the cost of production. But you could not call this a subsidy, because this situation has to be dealt with, and in a different manner from any other. The hon. member must realize that as far as gold mines are concerned the price of their product is strictly controlled, while the prices of all other products, such as milk, butter, steel, manufactured goods, or whatever you wish to name, have increased tremendously in the last few years.
Surely an industry that has given so much to the whole of our national life should be able to obtain some consideration from the government without unfair criticism. My hon. friend mentioned the dividends paid by the Hollinger mine. Does he realize that Hollinger is a low-grade mine? It is only because of the efficient management and working of this mine that they are able to pay these dividends. Has the hon. member taken the trouble to analyse what he calls the enormous profit of the Hollinger mine? Does he know the number of people who hold shares in this mine, and the heavy capital investments? Does he know that they are not paid a high rate of interest but a reasonable return on their investment?
The same thing applies to the McIntyre mine, which is only a few yards away from the Hollinger mine. It has higher grade ores

than the average mine, therefore the dividends have been a little higher than those paid by Hollinger. Why take a national forum such as this to attempt to create the impression that this important industry has been exploiting the federal treasury? I do not believe that that is fair. It is not my duty to defend the gold mining industry, because it needs no defenders. As a member who has represented for nearly a quarter of a century this great section of the country called the Porcupine, I know whereof I speak, and I am aware of the great benefits that accrued from this industry to every section of our population.
I remember when the McIntyre mine had to buy c.o.d. their lumber and all other required material. As in any other mining venture, they had to take a chance and invest their money, and believe me, it has not always been a winning gamble. If they are receiving dividends today, I do not see why these sinister motives should be imputed to them. I am speaking about these things feelingly, because I believe all our people should have justice from the central administration. I am astonished to hear a statement of the kind made by a practical member such as the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). A few years ago the same statement was repeated by a member in that group; he said that the gold mining industry was a sheltered industry. The gold mining industry is not sheltered, and does not want government protection; it only wants fair play.
I believe the passing of this bill is only fair play to the gold mining industry which means so much to the whole of our national economy. Its maintenance and future expansion will be important factors in Canada's prosperity.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I heartily support the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). He has firsthand information, and knows what he is talking about. During the depression there was no source of employment which could be compared with the gold mines in the north. I thank the hon. member for his statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who spent ten years underground at these northern Ontario gold mines, I should like to ask the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) if he has any idea how long it takes before a mine is in a position to pay dividends. It is impossible for a mine to sink a shaft, drive drifts, put in the raises, or employ any number of men before a period of from three to five years. As this subsidy is given to encourage development, I should like to point out to the member from
Gold Mining
the west that this is commendable legislation. It will provide employment during the next three or four years, when no doubt employment will be scarce. It will have a beneficial effect on our national economy, and I think it would be a shortsighted policy if we were to do anything that would curtail this development and thus lower employment in this country.
We all know that during the depressed years the gold mines were the greatest source of employment. For any party to suggest that we should discontinue legislation which would create jobs in from three to five years is not sensible.

speechtext: I am sure the hon. member did not hear me correctly. I did not suggest anything of the kind. I think this legislation for marginal mines should be kept on the statute book, but I do not believe-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
I
should like to say a few words on this measure, arising out of the remarks made by the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). I am afraid the misconception has arisen because of the reference to marginal mines rather than to marginal ore. The real intent of the bill is to encourage the production of gold in Canada. No matter how economists may rank the place of gold on the world exchange, there can be no doubt of the great value of high gold production to Canada in our foreign exchange problem.
There are two ways in which we can expand our gold production:	by giving
incentive to the small mines, giving them financial backing which will enable them to do extra exploration work, or-a much quicker way-by giving assistance which will encourage the larger mines to mine marginal ore. I am referring to ore which these mines

Gold Mining
have blocked out underground, but the marketing of which at a profit is doubtful. That is one of the two functions of this gold mining assistance act. While these are called subsidies, they would be much better regarded as incentives towards production. They act as an incentive to the small mines to explore and find new ore bodies, and to the large mines to bring to the surface the marginal ores which they would otherwise by-pass and leave below ground for all time. The large mines would take out the ore on which they could make a profit, and by-pass these large blocks of low-grade ore.
The success of this policy is shown in a report which no doubt the hon. member has seen. A subsidy was paid on the production over two-thirds of the base year. Last year it was paid on ninety per cent of the gold production in Canada-that is, from the primary producers. If there had been no increase in production over the base year, that subsidy would have been paid only on thirty-three per cent of the gold produced in Canada.
The whole of the hard rock mining industry has welcomed this act; and even the base metals mines, although they do not share in the subsidy, have welcomed it. They say that anything which encourages the gold mining industry encourages all hard rock mining, because gold has always been the lure for prospectors.
I can speak with some measure of authority, because a month ago I attended a meeting of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, and there was widespread appreciation of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and what it had accomplished in its primary purpose of increasing gold production in Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
As I see it, the crux of this question is whether the government has a policy of subsidy for the gold mining industry alone, or whether the sentiments expressed by the parliamentary assistant express government policy as applied to all industries. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) made it quite clear that he was quite satisfied that the marginal mines or mines under development should be given assistance until production begins. The figures he put on the record, however, clearly indicate that a large percentage of the assistance has gone to corporations that did not need it.
My particular approach to this problem concerns the government policy of no subsidies. I believe the government has made its position in this regard quite clear. In 1945 a production subsidy of approximately
[Mr. Sinclair.)
$8 million per year was provided for the coal mining industry, and that also was an incentive bonus; it was for the purpose of increasing production. But in 1945 the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, made it quiet clear that as far as the government was concerned they were through with that type of subsidy; it was no longer their policy. Early in 1946 when a subsidy of approximately $5 million was necessary to avoid upheaval in the mining industry in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance in this house were answering those of us who were arguing for that amount of subsidy in order to avoid a strike in the industry and enable both producer and operator to get back to a peacetime economy, they said: Oh, no; that is against government policy. The result was that these subsidies were withdrawn at that time and we in Nova Scotia went through a five months' strike in the industry which cost the communities in and around the coal mines millions of dollars, and they have not got over it yet.
I was surprised, therefore, when a few days ago a bill introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was passed which changes the subsidy policy to one of loan with regard to the coal industry. They say: No subsidy, but we will lend you money to develop; you pay that money back at a certain rate of interest. Certain stipulations are also made in that bill to see that the money is spent in such and such a way. If "lend" is the policy of the government with regard to the coal mines, and many of them are submarginal, and if "lend" is their policy in equipping them for increasing their production, why is that not the policy with regard to gold mining? Why should we have one mining industry in Canada receiving mother's allowance and another mining industry-which in my opinion is more essential to the economy of this country- denied that subsidy arrangement and put on a straight loan arrangement?
I am not arguing against that loan arrangement, because when people borrow money under a certain contract they will perhaps use it more carefully and get the greatest amount of good out of it. But you cannot have one policy for the gold mines in northern Ontario and another for the coal mines in eastern and western Canada. If there is any industry that would justify subsidies, it is the coal mining industry. You are not importing from the United States $200 million worth of gold a year, but you are importing that amount of coal each year

from the United States to Canada. If we in this house were alive to our own interests we should be creating incentive bonuses for the purpose of developing our coal industry in order to avoid the terrific drain of United States dollars from this country.
I have all the sympathy in the world for the hon. member (Mr. Hosking) who said he worked underground. But I want to tell him this: I do not think any of this money will benefit the man who works underground in these gold mines in central Canada.

speechtext: Dont be too sure about that.

I should like, Mr. Speaker, to answer in part the argument we have just heard from the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). It appears to me that he has completely ignored an important point made by the hon. member for Cochrane, namely, that the price of gold has remained static. In the gold mining industry you have a special case in which, for special reasons, the government have determined that the price of the product will remain static; and in a world of increasing costs, they have decided to give assistance to it in order that it can produce the product that it is considered desirable for the country to have. As long as the hon. member for Cape Breton South ignores this point he will never be able to give a clear and fair presentation of the case to this house.
Gold Mining
As to the coal mines and the importation of coal from the United States, surely the hon. member for Cape Breton South is aware of the fact that a large amount of the coal which is imported from the United States is anthracite, whereas the coal produced in his own constituency and thereabouts is bituminous, and in any event we are not in a position to compete with that imported coal.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I possibly cannot speak with as much authority on the subject as can the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), I do know something about gold mining. I worked in the gold mines for a considerable number of years. I have had occasion to visit every nook and corner of the gold mines of northern Ontario. I am fairly well acquainted with the management and the representatives of the workers in those mines.
Like the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), I want to make it clear first of all that personally I am not opposed to this bill. We are not opposed to assisting mines whose ore is of such a low grade that without some government assistance it could possibly not be mined at a profit. The shareholders who have been fortunate enough to hold the majority of the shares in these mines have not done too badly. I would say that by and large they have done much better than either the men who work underground in the mines or the municipalities in which the mines are situated.
If I were asking for a subsidy for the gold mining country, in addition to that which is paid to mines that actually need it in order to put them on a paying basis, it would not be for Hollinger, McIntyre or Teck-Hughes; it would be for the towns of Timmins and Kirkland Lake and the townships of Tisdale and

I have always deplored the enormous waste of energy represented by the production of gold. It is a commodity that rarely performs any useful service, because even in the early days there was far more gold than was needed to meet commercial needs. On the other hand, I do realize that so long as there are people and nations who actually desire to accept gold, it is definitely to the advantage of Canada to produce it so that we can export it and get goods and services in return.
While it is argued that gold mines are getting a special privilege in receiving a subsidy, we must not lose sight of the fact that the price of gold today is being held down at a much lower figure than would be the case if it were turned free. That is being done, of course, under the international monetary fund. It certainly would be to the advantage of the sterling area today to have gold turned free. It would make it possible for the sterling area to bring about a far better balance in international payments if the price of gold were allowed to rise to the price that it would reach if it were released from the international monetary fund. I suppose the members of the international monetary fund could accomplish that if they exerted a certain amount of pressure. It is easy to realize why the United States opposes such action; it is because the United States is the main purchaser of gold today. But I do believe that so long as the price of gold is held down under the international monetary fund the gold mines are justified in receiving a subsidy, because gold mining is one of the few industries today that has a ceiling on the price of the commodity it produces. That ceiling was set many years ago. Since that time the price of everything else has gone up. The price of gold has been held down. For this reason I think there is a justification for the subsidy.

Being an amateur in gold mining I assume that these bonuses have been given to Hollin-ger and the big shots for the production of gold. I assume they have been given for the production of more gold in this country, which we all admit we need, on the same basis as the subsidies which have been going to the smaller mines. subtopic: VALUE FOR DUTY OF GOODS IMPORTED

Mr. Chairman, this section is in general terms, but as it is short I shall read it:
(5) The governor in council may order that import duties of a country of export shall be disregarded, in whole or in part, in estimating the value for duty of goods of any kind imported into Canada from a country specified in the order.
During the Senate debate on this bill Senator Hugessen said:
I am advised that West Indies rum and Irish whiskey are imported in large bulk quantities by England, that they are aged and bottled in England, and thereafter are exported to Canada.
Senator Hugessen went on to explain that the same was true of other wines and sherries, and he intimated that the bill was intended to deal with that particular situation. At the end of his explanation Senator Hugessen said that the class of commodity sought to be covered by this legislation might vary from time to time. I am advised that the reason for this change is mainly, if not exclusively, that given by Senator Hugessen. I am not suggesting that the legislation can be amended at this late date, but I am wondering if it would not be possible for the minister to indicate that that is what is intended, that the section will be used for that purpose.
It seems to me to be most undesirable to have a section in a statute as wide as this. After all, it will throw considerable uncertainty into business. If in fact it is intended to cover this one case I hope the minister may see fit to give a firm assurance that that is what is intended.

subtopic: VALUE FOR DUTY OF GOODS IMPORTED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel that I can give the assurance that what is indicated by the hon. member for Greenwood is the purpose for which the section is intended. Perhaps I could put on the record the main

Customs Act
purposes of this bill, in order that there may be a clearer understanding when we are discussing other sections.
The purpose of section 1 is to make it possible to disregard, in the determination of value for Canadian customs duty, all or part of the import duties of the country of export. At present the inclusion of these figures in the calculation of the value for duty is said to be not only unfair but also a deterrent to the export and sale to Canada of certain British goods at a time when trade between Britain and Canada is so vital to both countries and when international agreements are being drawn up to remove unreasonable administrative barriers to international trade.
In determining the value for duty of domestic products of Great Britain entering Canada, the Canadian customs, by law, disregards the internal excise taxes of the exporting country; but should the goods exported from Britain not be of domestic origin, Canadian customs have to include in its determination of value for duty the amount of import duties applicable in Great Britain, even though such duties had never been applied to the goods.
The explanation is that a lot of these goods come from other countries to Great Britain, are put in bond and actually do not pay these taxes, which for the most part are luxury taxes. They are then processed and shipped to this country. According to the act we do not regard those taxes that are put on there, but we have to take into account for customs purposes, when the goods come into Canada, not only the price of the goods but the duties that are levied in Great Britain.
There is an obvious anomaly here between the excise taxes and the customs duties which is most striking when the import duties and internal excise tax of the exporting country bear a direct relationship, and equal or nearly equal each other. The ultimate result of the present method of determining value for duty is to cause an increase in the figure on which the Canadian sales tax-I ask hon. members to note this-is applied; for, as is generally known, the sales tax on imported goods is based on the value for duty as established for customs purposes. The application of the tax on this basis obviously increases the price to the customer.
The proposed amendment is merely an extension of the principle in the law by which excise taxes of the exporting country are disregarded in determining value for duty in Canada. Import duties of the exporting country could, under this section, be

treated in a similar manner when such action is deemed advisable by the governor in council. Thus any anomaly or unfairness would be removed and the goods enabled to be entered and marketed at competitive prices.
I think I might also deal at the present time with the principles of the other sections of the bill. Sections 2 and 3 provide for the repeal of certain sections of the act which still contain titles of offices which have been abolished, and for the substitution for these sections of a more uniform and standardized wording in line with modern drafting principles. These proposed amendments carry no substantive changes of law. It is only a tidying up process.
With reference to the fourth section of the bill, it is an amendment which is intended to make an appeal procedure available to the innocent owner of a vehicle or vessel seized and confiscated under the Customs Act, which at the present time disregards entirely the question of ownership in such cases. This provision is similar to section 169(a) of the Excise Tax Act, which was enacted in 1934 in order to enable the innocent owner, mortgagee or lien holder to appeal to the courts to protect his interests or equity in the vehicle seized. I think it will be seen that the present law rather creates an injustice to the innocent owner of a seized automobile which has been used for smuggling purposes. Perhaps some acceptance corporation or other person has a lien against the vehicle. When it is seized it becomes forfeited and is sold, and the person who has a lien, or who has not yet been paid for the vehicle which has been confiscated, suffers the entire loss of his equity in it. The purpose of the amendment is to give that person or corporation an opportunity to appeal to the courts to protect his lien.

I desire to speak briefly, and largely about one aspect of the labour question which I think will develop as I proceed.
It is very late in the history of the world to review industrial relations between capital-and I still like that word-and labour. I begin by reaffirming a belief, which I have held for many years, and which I have proved by my actions, in the unionization or organization of labour in industry. I arrive at that conclusion from some knowledge of the question, and it seems to me also from sheer reason.
We all know that the organization of labour into unions has done much to improve
Supply-Labour
their position, in Canada as well as in other countries. There was a time when labour was regarded simply as an intake product in whatever industry labour had to be used. For a long time industry fought the organization of labour. I am happy to say that in Canada that day has long since gone. I think industry has learned that it is better off when labour is so organized. There are still a few who endeavour, as we heard this morning, to stop the organization of labour in various plants. Fortunately they are few in this day and generation. I frankly admit that errors have been made in union policy, but the general good that has come to the community through such organizations far outweighs any mistakes that were made in times gone by.
We may compliment ourselves that in this country today we have practically no strikes, and very little unrest in the ranks of labour. In discussing the estimates that are before us we shall wish to know a number of things which I have no intention of discussing now: but we might remember that the taxpayers of this country are paying a tremendous sum of money in this connection. This year it is $49,629,156, an increase of $806,567 over last year; but perhaps the explanations may wait until we are considering the estimates item by item.
I wish also to pay a sincere compliment to organized labour in Canada on what it has done with respect to communism. Labour has purged itself much better than it could be done by any law passed by this or any other government. The men who led that battle and who received much abuse, some of it physical, in reaching that great objective, are worthy of the highest commendation this house can give them.
I should like also to try to destroy the fiction which is in the minds of many people in this country, as a result of which communism comes to their thoughts whenever labour is mentioned. It is true that labour provides a field in which that vile thing might grow; but let us not think for a moment that labour itself is the chief source of communists. It is not. The chief source of communists, I am sorry to say, is among well-educated people, many of them in our institutions of learning, people who should know much better. I am anxious to go on record definitely as saying that while progress was made in a fruitful field-and we all know the reasons for that, highly uninformed as some of these persons are-the leadership had to come from somewhere else; and it came from well-educated people in this country rather than from labour itself.

Supply-Labour
I am going to say nothing more, Mr. Chairman, except that we shall examine the estimates and be sceptical about an increase of almost a million dollars. Today the administration is not faced with the problems it had to deal with last year or the year before. I am happy to know that all of us in this house played some part in the creation of what might well be called a labour code in Canada. No one in this house can claim the entire credit for that, because, as the minister well knows, and as I credit him with having said, it was threshed out by a large group of people from this house who were aiming to do only one thing, that is, something which might be valuable in settling labour disputes and quieting unrest and disaffection among those of us who work with our hands for our living.
Now I have finished, and shall content myself with an examination of the estimates item by item.

subtopic: VALUE FOR DUTY OF GOODS IMPORTED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to be able to associate myself with almost everything the hon. member for Calgary West has said. As a matter of fact the first thought that came to my mind as the minister and the committee prepared to deal with these estimates was to congratulate the minister and the country on the very few labour disputes we have had during the present year. Compared with the difficult times the minister had in previous years I think he has had a very easy time of it lately. I hope he does not grow too fat and complacent on it, because if he has had an easy time there are others who have not had it quite so easy.
I was glad the hon. member for Calgary West mentioned the steps taken by labour bodies to lessen the influence of communists in their organizations, and I want to point out that this was no easy task to undertake. It meant that people had to be dealt with because of political opinions. It is not so very long ago that I heard responsible leaders in the labour movement say, and quite correctly at that time, that they would not interfere with a man's position in the labour movement because of his political opinions, no matter what those opinions might be. The sad thing about communists, however, is that we cannot deal with them as we would deal with ordinary people, because they do not act as ordinary people do. That is the position with which the labour movement was confronted, and it took a great deal of courage to handle it in the way it was handled.
The principal reason why I rise to speak on these estimates is that I have been receiving communications from various parts of Canada, and particularly from the

province of British Columbia. I am concerned about the unemployment situation this winter in my province, and what is to be done to meet it. I do not want it to be taken that I expect an unemployment situation of huge proportions, or on a scale such as we had during the depression years. I do not think we shall have that this winter, but unemployment worked a great hardship among the people of British Columbia last winter. The situation will be considerably worse this winter. I believe that will be so, not only in British Columbia but right across Canada.
Hon. members will have noted that I put questions on the order paper recently, which were answered on November 24, that is, less than two weeks ago. I asked as to the comparative number of persons receiving unemployment insurance in September and October of 1948 and 1949. While the number is not particularly large, the increase this year over last is, to me, alarming. I shall give the figures to hon. members so that they may have them in mind. In 1948 the number of persons receiving unemployment insurance totalled 44,000 in September, and
55.000	in October-I am giving the round figures. In 1949 the figures were 83,000 in September and 105,000 in October-that is, they had almost doubled.
This is only the beginning of the decline in employment. I have noticed that in other years unemployment reached its peak in February or March, and then began to drop until about August. I asked a similar question about new applications received for unemployment insurance in September and October of 1948 and 1949. We find the same situation. In September, 1948, there were
28.000 new applications; and in October,
38.000.	In September, 1949, there were
51.000,	and in October, 69,000. It seems to me that is a steep increase in the number of those making application for unemployment insurance. These figures do not include unemployed persons who are not covered by unemployment insurance, and a large number of the workers are not covered.
Representations were made to me by the British Columbia command of the Canadian Legion, and by the two central labour bodies in Vancouver. I have noticed that the Canadian Legion is running advertisements in the daily papers in Vancouver to draw attention to the situation. Will the minister say whether any preparations are being made to provide assistance to those unemployed employables who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits?
I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that it will be harder

for the municipalities to look after the unemployed who are not receiving unemployment insurance, not only because of their numbers but because, in almost every city, the welfare agencies have found it more difficult to raise funds this year. Then again, we must remember that the unemployment insurance benefits are hardly sufficient-I said hardly sufficient, but I think I can make it much stronger than that. With the present prices, they are not sufficient to maintain a family. Assistance must come from some other source. I should be glad indeed if the minister could give some assurance to the committee that the government is planning for this need.
I believe the committee should be informed that less food is being purchased now than during 1947. The volume of food sales is lower than in 1947. I believe most of the members receive the Financial Times. In the copy which came to my desk yesterday, there is a chart showing the trend of food sales in 1947, 1948, and 1949. The sales in terms of dollars showed a steep increase-from an index figure of 90 to 120 since the beginning of 1947. In physical volume, however, the trend has been the other way. As a matter of fact the graph forms a triangle. Beginning at 90, one leg of the triangle goes up to 120 and the other goes down to almost 80. This indicates, Mr. Chairman, that the standard of living is going down, and that it is exceedingly important that this winter the government should, either by financial assistance or by providing work projects, ease the burden on persons who are unemployed. It should also ease the burden of the municipalities concerned, because they will not be able to handle the situation which will shortly confront them.

There are many things that could be said in a general way on the
Supply-Labour
minister's estimates, but I think a good deal of it can be reserved for the items as we come to them.
A great deal of progress has been made in the Department of Labour since I first came into the house, if one just stops and thinks back; and there is no harm in recalling exactly what has taken place in the last ten years. I know that the Department of Labour today is about a hundred per cent more efficient than it was when I came into this house in 1940.

subtopic: VALUE FOR DUTY OF GOODS IMPORTED
speechtext: See what you have done for it.

subtopic: VALUE FOR DUTY OF GOODS IMPORTED
speechtext:
It was not necessarily what I did, or what the minister did. He has been fortunate in getting into the department persons who know a great deal about the problem and are anxious to do something about it. The credit goes to no one person, but if any credit is due to an individual I would give it to the deputy minister. The deputy minister is the brains of any department. In addition he must have a flexible minister. Either the Minister of Labour is flexible or the deputy minister is a good diplomat, because he has been responsible for getting a good deal done. We on this side of the house of course have provoked their thoughts, pushed them along and perhaps given them some ideas.
When I came into the house in 1940 we had no Unemployment Insurance Act. Today we have such an act, and I think it is working reasonably well. It needs some jacking up here and there, but we shall reserve discussion on that matter until we come to the item dealing with it. The national employment offices across the country, which have been built up under the machinery in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Act, are a valuable asset if they are used for the purpose for which they were intended. During the war these offices had the right to direct employees and the right to file the requirements of the employers. During the war I think they did an excellent job in directing employees and assisting people to to go from one section of the country to another where there was employment in the particular trades in which they were interested. Since the war these offices have lost that function.
The employment offices have an excellent set-up. They have registered all unemployed who come under the act, and the trades or jobs for which they are fitted; but they no longer have the right to direct employees, and the employer is under no obligation to register his needs. From close contacts with those offices I know that they are working under a handicap in that respect. Many

Supply-Labour
unemployed are not registered because they do not come under the act, and they are wandering around in a circle, whereas if they could go to these offices and get direction, the officers would be performing a much more useful function.
In 1940 we had no national labour code. We now have a code which is national in scope. We have at least established the principle. But that act also, in my opinion, requires some amendment. We have not only suggested amendments but we have moved bills in the house. I think it requires an amendment to provide that the Canada labour board shall be in a position to enforce the act by initiating prosecution when an infraction of the act is committed. I am not going to argue that point again. I maintained it on two occasions in the house by moving a bill. I still hope for that amendment. I am reasonably sure that at some time in the future such a provision will be written into the national code.
I think the act also needs amendment in the matter of the voluntary revocable checkoff. I think that too will come in time. It is the minimum measure of union security that we can hope for in legislation. It would be of great benefit to the trade union movement across the country.
A definition of employees is necessary. There should be a broader definition than is there now; because an employer is in a position to put a fairly wide interpretation on the present definition of an employee who is eligible for membership in a union under the code. He can classify practically anyone in a plant or factory as being ineligible because he is engaged in a confidential capacity. I am not going to argue that point now either. The arguments are on the record. I know that the labour department know what they are. In time I think we may be able to cure the code in that respect.
The most important question that today faces the Department of Labour and the workers of this country generally is the matter of industrial pensions. The main emphasis across the country in every section of labour, be it organized or unorganized, is the necessity of security against the time when they are no longer able to provide for themselves. Last night in the committee on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, I listened to a discussion on industrial pensions and their relationship to that department. I did not take part in it because I felt that it was out of order. I believe, however, that it is the responsibility of the Department of Labour to lay the basis for some uniform national scheme of industrial pensions.
[Mr. Gillis.I
Right now there are a great many disconnected schemes. Industry after industry is establishing some kind of scheme of its own; but in my opinion there can be no solution to the problem on that basis. As I have previously pointed out in the house, an industry such as the pulp and paper industry in Canada can provide a decent pension, and they have done so. They pay $100 a month after a certain number of years' service; they protect the widow after the husband passes on; they have an excellent scheme. They can handle a scheme of that kind because the industry has the income with which to do it. But there are hundreds of industries in this country, some small and some large, which have not the income, through profits, to set up a decent pension scheme. They are essential industries, but they do not make large profits. The great majority of the workers of this country work in the kind of industry that cannot provide an industrial pension for them.
Another thing that focuses attention on the problem is the policy of industry itself. Since the end of the war they have taken the position that they will not employ anyone over forty years of age. If a man who is forty years of age is out of work today, and has not some specialized training, he will not be taken on by any industry in which the labour is fairly heavy, such as the mining, steel or automobile industries. He will not receive employment. There is growing up in this country a group of thousands and thousands of men who in the past have contributed something to some industry, who get out of work for some reason or another and cannot be employed. The heavy industries have taken the position that when a man is sixty-five years of age he is pensioned off. In most cases where that takes place, particularly in the mining industry, there is no contributory system of pensions. The companies have established some schemes of their own which are non-contributory. It is something they pay themselves as a gratuity. It cannot be called a pension. It is based on twenty-five years' service and on a small percentage of the last ten years of employment when earnings were the lowest. It amounts to about $15 a month up to a maximum of $57 or $60 a month. But in that scheme the over-all average, as applied to steel and coal in Nova Scotia, would run around $30 a month. That is nothing to look forward to. The man is back on relief.
The Canadian Congress of Labour have taken this position. To continue to probe the matter and to find a solution as from industry to industry in Canada means that all you will succeed in doing will be to set up the differentials in pensions that exist in

wage rates across the country at the present time. That is what will happen if a contributory scheme of pensions is established. On the other hand many industries cannot provide any pension at all. My considered opinion is, and has been for a long time, that the only way you can establish a fair retiring allowance for industrial workers in this country and for white-collar workers is to recognize the principle of social security.
I believe the department is now working on this question. I know the minister has one of his officials in Nova Scotia lecturing on industrial pensions. I do not know what the scheme is, but the minister will likely refer to it later. Now that the labour department has begun to gather statistics on the problem, the minister should consider this aspect of it: the only way to answer the question for the workers across this country -I do not mean just those who use a pick and shovel; I mean civil servants and all those who are white-collar workers in industry-is to establish a social security tax. I am not going to say what the amount should be. Everyone in the country should pay a tax, and it should be earmarked as a retiring allowance and set to one side and supplemented out of the consolidated revenue fund. The employer and the employee would contribute to it. The worker would then know that when he had worked for a certain number of years in industry he would be paying a special tax. I can assure the committee that nobody would object to a special tax for that purpose. It would be on a national basis. There would be one administration, and competent people in the annuities branch could work it out, thus eliminating the wasting of millions of dollars by industry in the maintenance of administrative staffs to work out the small and inadequate pensions that exist today.
The one thing that keeps most people in life worried and sends them to an early grave is insecurity. The average worker can pay only enough by way of insurance premiums to guarantee his family that at least there will be sufficient money to bury him when he dies. He is worried all the time on that score. At the convention in Toronto a year ago the Canadian Congress of Labour changed a resolution they had on industrial pensions to read the way I have suggested. They said that from then on the labour organizations should concentrate on a drive to sell the federal government the idea of a national social security tax to provide retiring allowances to workers in every industry and in every profession. I do not say what the contribution should be, but in my opinion that is the only kind of contributory scheme of pensions that will work, and it is the kind 45781-169
Supply-Labour
of thing that most people are thinking about and working for in a piecemeal and disjointed way at this time.
I do not expect the minister to say that this kind of thing will be done. I am speaking about it now so that people may think about it. If we are honestly of the opinion that something should be done in that field, I think that is the only way it can be done. It would answer the question of old age pensions, which we are wrangling about all the time, and the means test. The workers of this country do not want charity. When they retire after producing the wealth of the country they do not want to have to go to some charitable organization and qualify for the means of existence. Because of the means test in old age pensions, they are up against that very thing. Somebody has to come in and ascertain whether, because of the clothes in your cupboard and your living accommodation, you should receive something which is on the basis of charity. If my suggestion were adopted, that would be overcome.
On the other hand, large contributions are made to charitable organizations for the purpose of looking after the aged, the infirm and the afflicted. Nobody wants to accept the kind of charity which is handed out by the Red Cross, the Blue Cross, the White Cross, and all of these other organizations. Nobody wants to end his days by having to accept charity on that basis. In my opinion the only way to eliminate it is to give people a chance, by way of a special tax, to contribute to a national scheme and place the money in the hands of a competent administration that can work the matter out on an actuarial basis and determine exactly what the employee's contribution would be, what industry's should be and how much should come out of the consolidated revenue fund. Make it not just another tax, but a social security tax set to one side for that purpose. It would be pretty much a duplication of the unemployment insurance fund. It might be handled by that department. I do not think it would require additional staff.

Mr. Chairman, when we took recess for lunch I was making a few general observations. I was elaborating on the question of industrial pensions, which I consider to be one of the objectives of the labour program. I am not going to repeat what I said previously, but I wish to add that I think Canada is in a good position to make a judgment on this particular development.

Supply-Labour
We have the experience of the commonwealth countries to draw from, as well as those of another country which is closer to us and whose economy is pretty much the same as ours, the United States.
But I think what is happening in the United States is proof positive that the establishment of pension plans by industry is not working out. The mine workers were the first union to have a pension of $100 a month established, but the net result has been the creation of one of the greatest obstacles to industrial harmony between employer and employee that has arisen since the establishment of the labour movement. Any industry which cannot pass along to the consumer the additional cost of such a pension plan will not be able to carry it out. When the time comes that they cannot pass it along to the consumer, difficulties arise. The pension plan established by the mine workers worked for one year while it was in the embryo stage, but during the last year there has been a continual disruption of that industry in an effort to maintain the pension of $100 a month.
I think this is a fair indication that we cannot follow along that road with any degree of success and hope to maintain harmonious relations between labour and management. Within the past few months the steel industry in the United States have established a pension plan, and I know they will have great difficulty in trying to maintain it. The automobile workers in Canada are following the pattern set in the United States. In my opinion the only way it can be done in this or any other country is not to pass the cost along to the consumer, but to establish a national security plan which will be supported by contributions by the worker, the employer and to some extent from the consolidated revenue fund. The plan should have the efficient administration we now have in the annuities branch. I know this will not happen tomorrow, I know there will be much difficulty in selling the idea to members of the government, but someone or some group must be looking forward in the field of social legislation and be ready to support it.
I shall not make any further general remarks, but there are many small problems that will be discussed when we reach the appropriate items.

Mr. Chairman, under this general administration item I should like to deal with another branch of the department, the training branch. First of all I should like to compliment the minister and his officers upon the excellent job they have done in vocational training.

There are two schools of thought about education; there are those who believe that education consists chiefly of academic training, and there are those who are interested in vocational training. I was an academic teacher for close to twenty years. I taught in schools where the great majority of the pupils came from industrial homes, and I have learned to appreciate the need and the value of training that our boys and girls are getting in the vocational schools.
According to the report of the department, from the inception of the dominion-provincial training plan in 1937 up to March 31, 1949, there has been an enrolment of 918,740 pupils, close to one million young people who have been benefited by that training during those years. In the last fiscal year the enrolment in these courses was 23,891, with an expenditure of $9,133,300.
I should like to deal briefly with the different types of vocational work that has been carried on. First I want to express my regret that the province of Ontario did not take advantage of the youth training plan over the years. However, last year they availed themselves of the $50,000 that was allotted for youth training which was used to aid students in colleges, universities, nursing training schools, and so forth.
In the field of supervisory training, I note with the same regret that Ontario has indicated that this will be discontinued during the coming year. The report indicates that great assistance has been given in supervisory training, particularly during the past year. Last year three provinces were allotted money, but in no case did a province use the full allotment. Of the $9,000 allotted to Ontario for supervisory training, the province availed itself of only $2,534. Of the $9,000 allotted to the province of Quebec, the province availed itself of $5,867. Of the $3,000 allotted to British Columbia for this type of training, the province availed itself of $1,080.
According to the report this money was used for the training of industrial supervisors and personnel officials; education in job relations and job methods; to aid job safety institutes, and for conferences pertaining to these subjects. There is a great need, particularly in the industrial provinces, for the type of work the act is designed to support, and I feel that this need is as great as it ever has been. Again I regret to see that the province of Ontario has indicated its intention to discontinue that field this year. I notice that the training given to the armed forces, which during the past year absorbed over $3 million, will not necessarily be carried on because that particular phase of the

work is completed. I was hopeful that the minister would be able to secure the $3 million for his department in order that it might be transferred to other fields of education, but I see no indication in the estimates of that being done.
There is another phase of work carried on by the department in which I am interested, the training of unemployed persons. Here again I notice in the report that, while money was available to all the provinces for the vocational training of unemployed persons, there were three provinces in Canada which did not avail themselves of that assistance, Prince Edward Island, Quebec and Ontario. I gather from the report, however, that the training of unemployed personnel was carried on in the province of Quebec to a large extent with assistance from the federal government in the regular vocational schools of the province. Once again I am at a loss to know why, with the number of unemployed increasing in the province of Ontario, the provincial government has not availed itself fully of the assistance for the training of unemployed persons through the regular vocational schools of the province.
Before I deal with the financial assistance given to vocational schools, there is another point in the report to which I wish to refer, the replacement of depreciated equipment within the vocational schools of the country. I find there was a total amount of $259,600 approved by the minister for replacing such equipment in our technical schools, but there were certain strings attached to that. The act gives the minister authority to refund to certain schools 75 per cent of the cost of equipment purchased by them from War Assets Corporation up to the total amount of $259,600 approved by the minister. The report goes on to say that few claims have been sent in by the schools to which funds were made available, and that total payments up to the present time have been $73,423 as against the $259,600 allotted. Of the $73,423, $25,584 was paid during the last fiscal year to one school in Nova Scotia, two in Ontario, three in Saskatchewan and three in British Columbia. I note the reason given why more of these funds were not used is that War Assets Corporation has been able to supply little suitable equipment.
While the minister is speaking on his estimates, I should like him to tell us why it was that War Assets Corporation was able to supply so little equipment to our vocational schools. I cannot believe the reason is that such equipment did not exist. During the war years I had the privilege of visiting a great many of the war industry plants in Ontario.
Supply-Labour
I know something about the type of equipment used in our vocational schools, and I am confident there must have been a great deal of war assets equipment that would have been suitable for use. Because War Assets Corporation was able to supply very little I note that the provinces have only been able to avail themselves of $73,423 when the department had an amount allotted of $259,600.
I want to touch briefly on two major fields in which the department is contributing so far as vocational training is concerned. One that I overlooked is apprentice training. From the report it is evident that valuable work has been done in that field. During the fiscal year ending March, 1948, 6,286 apprentices have been assisted under the act, 3,659 of them in the province of Ontario. I also notice that for the year 1949 there has been a considerable drop in the number of apprentices who received assistance under the act. I am quite sure the minister will want to give us some explanation why there is a decreasing number of apprentices taking advantage of the privileges afforded by the legislation.
The department's greatest assistance to vocational education was in the direct contributions made to the provinces for regular vocational training in their schools. An agreement was made with the provinces whereby there was to be an annual outright grant of $10,000 to each province, which was not to be matched. It was an outright gift to each of the provinces to be used by them in vocational education. A grant was made over a ten-year period of $1,910,000 which was to be used in the development of vocational education, and there was a special contribution of $10 million to be allotted among the provinces for capital expenditures on the building and; equipment of vocational schools. There is noquestion but that the assistance given has aided the advancement of vocational education across Canada. I am sure that the minister with his background is probably as-sympathetic to the development of vocational education as any other hon. member in the house.
I would like to call to his attention this report, which indicates that as a result of those direct grants given to the provinces prior to April 1, 1948, in addition to the schools which had been assisted there were 116 schools either completed, in process of completion or approved by the department for assistance under this act, which means that fifty per cent of the cost of constructing and equipping those 116 schools across Canada would come from these funds. In his report the minister told us that in addition.

Supply-Labour
to those 116 schools there were 79 new buildings or additions to existing buildings planned by municipalities, which would be built without assistance from the department.
I want to bring to the attention of the committee a resolution which was adopted by the vocational training advisory committee, a special committee set up under the act to advise the minister and the department with respect to its administration. At its meeting on October 4, 1948, that advisory committee called attention to the fact that since this act came into force in 1945 the cost of building and equipping vocational schools had increased greatly, and that the original amount voted for this purpose fell far short of achieving what those who put through this legislation had in mind. As a result of increased construction costs, fewer schools could be built than the government and the department visualized in 1945.
In view of that condition the committee recommended that a further grant of $5 million be made by the dominion for capital expenditure, to be distributed on the same basis as the earlier capital grant; and that annual grants should be increased from $2 million to $4 million. The committee felt this would be effective in carrying out the objectives of the department as set forth in the original act. I have looked through the estimates for this year and find that while the department has been able to reduce its estimates for vocational training by some $3 million because of the fact that it is not required to provide that training for those coming out of the armed forces, there is nothing in the estimates to indicate that this recommendation of the advisory committee has been accepted. The report to which I am referring states that as of March 31, 1949, those recommendations were still under consideration.
As I have already indicated, I am quite sure the minister personally is very sympathetic to this work. I am convinced that if his wishes could prevail in the cabinet the recommendations of this committee would be adopted. So I want to say, not so much to the minister as to the other members of the cabinet who help determine government policy and government budgets, that here is one field where government money can be spent to good advantage to assist the boys and girls of this country. This is one field in which there is no quarrel with the provinces. One feature of these vocational training grants is the way in which this government has been able to co-operate with all the provincial governments in the field of vocational

education. I am assured by provincial educational officers and by officers of the minister's department that there has been nothing but the utmost co-operation in this field.
There are communities where vocational education is badly needed. I think of the community from which I come, the township of York. There we have an industrial population of close to one hundred thousand, with somewhere around four thousand boys and girls attending secondary schools. There we have no vocational school or vocational class of any kind. These thousands of pupils, coming from industrial homes, can get only an academic education leading to matriculation. In that community only about ten per cent of those who enter the secondary schools continue through to grade XIII, and less than two per cent of the pupils proceed to university. That is the sort of community where there is a crying need for vocational education. The township of York is one of the suburbs of Toronto. Most of the large business firms are located in Toronto, and much of the money of that community is spent in that city. Toronto derives taxation from all the large industrial and business centres, which are supported by the suburban communities. The schools of my community derive their support almost entirely from two sources, the assistance given by the provincial government and the taxes on the homes and properties of that area.
It had been planned to build a vocational school there to accommodate a thousand pupils. Today in the township of York there are well over a thousand pupils who would attend a vocational school if one were available. They were unable to get their plans to the department here before the expiration of the period for application. As a result the best that community can do without aid from the federal government will be to construct a school for five or six hundred pupils instead of a thousand, a school without a gymnasium or an auditorium, and without much of the equipment that is absolutely necessary for a vocational school. Were the department or the government to take into consideration the recommendation of this vocational advisory committee, and to include, if not in this year's estimates certainly in next year's, the extra moneys recommended, the community of York township, and many of these other 70 communities across Canada who are undertaking to build vocational schools without any federal assistance, would be able to build better schools in those communities. Those schools would be able to carry on that particular type of work more effectively.

It was my desire to call this matter to the government's attention, and I hope to hear from the minister when he speaks, whether or not his department has taken this recommendation into consideration; and whether or not they are likely to have included in the estimates grants that will make it possible for many of these communities across Canada to get further assistance.

I have been interested in the discussion thus far, and I was particularly interested in the contribution made by the member for Vancouver East and the member for Cape Breton South. Perhaps I did not see just as deeply into the general current of the thinking of those gentlemen as I should have, but it seems to me they were advocating policies which were contradictory. This is a solemn warning to the members of this house, as representatives of the community of Canada. Something must be done about that. Obviously, if the trend continues, a disaster of one kind or another will result.
Evidently the member for Vancouver East had in mind some measure for reducing the cost of living. I am in hearty accord with him in that objective. This immediately poses the question of how this cost of living is to be reduced. How are you going to bring down the retail prices in Canada? It is well known that if the labouring men strike to raise wages, immediately there will be another spiral of increased costs. If the labouring men do not strike, but continue with the wages they are now receiving, and the prices continue much as they are, then a generation of young Canadians will almost assuredly suffer far more seriously than this house would care to contemplate. If we can determine now where the money is coming from with which to pay the dividend, then our thinking can go forward another milepost. What the hon. member for Vancouver East really has in mind is what the Social Crediters call the just price, which is brought about by a compensated discount which reduces the price to the consumer. The hon. member for Vancouver East is therefore well along his way toward progressive thinking as Social Crediters look upon it. I rather think that most members on both sides of the house, both Liberals and Conservatives, would favour a reduction in price by a compensated discount, for the Liberals used it with regard to many commodities during the war, and with great success. It is too bad that they did not continue so to control price after the war. They seemed to assume
'Mr. Blackmore.]
that as soon as the war was over all further problems in regard to price had ceased. In reality, those problems had only just begun. No proposal has yet been brought forward for the systematic reduction of prices, notwithstanding the fact that prices are just torturing people from coast to coast in Canada. What the hon. member for Cape Breton South was advocating was a dividend for all or at least a dividend for all those who had found it necessary, for one reason or another, to leave industry.
May I suggest to the members of the committee and to these two good gentlemen and their colleagues in parliament that money can be obtained out of production. I have heard them, in some of their moments of illumination, state that financing would be done out of production; but what they seemed to have in mind was out of taxing production. The thing our generation must realize is that you do not need to tax production in order to get money. If the producers are producing ample goods, let them produce the goods and let the government use the goods as a basis for money. In this way a government can finance projects out of production without injuring the producer or the consumer. Once this committee learns that, and once the government learns that, with all the high ideals that are actuating the government and the opposition today, Canada will be on her way to an era of prosperity and happiness that we have dreamed about in times past but have never dared to hope we would realize.
