On section 7-Depreciation.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister whether this would be the place for him to make some reference to the new system of depreciation which has been proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Probably this would be as good a place as any. In my budget speech on March 22, I referred to the general principle of the new basis on which depreciation would be allowed. It will be found on page 1799 of Hansard. Perhaps my hon. friend has read it, and I do not know that it is necessary for me to repeat it now, but it might be as well if I were to do that. At that time I said:
In the past allowances have been granted on the basis of wear and tear of assets used in earning the income subject to tax. Under the new regulations which my colleague the Minister of National Revenue is proposing, the governing principle will be the amortization of costs of depreciable assets. Incidentally, an effect of this will be to allow for obsolescence hitherto unrecognized under our act. In the second place the rates of write-off will apply to the written-down value of the asset account rather than to the total asset account. In the technical language of the accountant this means changing from the straight-line method of depreciation to the diminishing balance principle. Of course the rates of depreciation will be appropriately increased having regard to the diminishing base to which they apply. Thirdly, it is proposed to introduce what might loosely be described as a recapture provision. This provision will operate to ensure in effect that the deductions for amortizing the cost of an asset shall not exceed the final proven cost of the asset to the taxpayer. It will call for an adjustment against future write-offs where assets are disposed of after wme use. I might add here that the so-called add-back or adjustment will be limited to the written-down value at the end of 1948 regardless of the price realized on disposal of assets in order that there can be no possible claim that under this provision capital gains are being taxed, or that this recapture provision has any retroactive effect.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Will the minister explain it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants me to explain it, I shall be delighted to take a long time to do it, but I do not think he really wants me to do so. He knows as well as I do that the matter is an extremely technical one. The Minister of National Revenue and his officials have been engaged for some time in the preparation of the necessary detailed regulations to outline the basis upon which the new system will operate.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Will the minister give a concrete example?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, I think perhaps I could do that. Take the case of an asset which cost the taxpayer $100,000. Rates of depreciation are established under the regulations to be enacted of, let us say, 15 per cent per annum. The asset as acquired is held by the taxpayer

for five years. It will then have been written down to 25 per cent of its original value or, in other words, $25,000.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is on straight line depreciation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is on straight line depreciation; my hon. friend is quite right. It would start off at 15 per cent, and there would be varying percentages down through the years. The 15 per cent would be applied each year to the depreciated value of the asset and at the end of, let us say, five years it would have a value on the books of whatever you like, say, $25,000 or $30,000. Then it is sold for $50,000 and in virtue of the recapture provision to which I have referred, the $20,000 would have to be taken up into profit and loss and would of course be subject to tax in the year in which it is taken. That is a fairly simple example. I understand that in more complicated cases it could be much more complex than that, but I think it illustrates the principle to which I am referring.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Regulations are now being made in detail which will govern this exceedingly important and vital thing. At what point does the house get a chance to see them? At what point do we get a chance to study them? Or are we just to take them on the minister's short, though highly interesting statement? I think it is a matter of great concern. As the minister knows, I have been trying to get these regulations for the last couple of weeks. It would be a natural thing for us to want to study them and even to confer with the business community and try to make sure that there was no suggestion that needed to be made. I understand that they are not even in print yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is correct. My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that they cannot be adopted by the governor in council until this particular section 7 is passed setting out some of the matters which must be spelt out in the law before the regulations can be adopted. My hon. friend will recall that until the amendment made to the Income Tax Act last year, the depreciation provisions were not even a matter of regulation. They were a matter of discretion. What will happen is this. After this law has been enacted, regulations prepared by the Department of National Revenue will be brought to the cabinet council, will be adopted, will then be published in the Canada Gazette and will be made available for all who are interested. They will then be subject to the general scrutiny of those who are interested, including the commercial community, lawyers, accountants and others who are considering these questions. So far as consideration by the house is concerned, I 45781-174
Income Tax Act
suppose they will not be available for reference and discussion here until the next session. But I point out to my hon. friend that under the act as adopted last year, and under the amendment which is proposed in this bill, and which is required in order to enable the regulations to be passed, it is provided that it will be done by regulation and not by ministerial discretion.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
But we are
in this absurd position now, apparently: the regulations cannot be approved until we approve this act; and we cannot see the regulations before we approve it, so we are approving something, in effect, where we have had nothing but a very sketchy illustration, if the minister will permit me to so describe it; and incidentally he gave us the wrong figures, although that is neither here nor there. But it seems to me that this important thing is being dealt with as if it were something of trifling importance that is just done every day by the officials in their stride.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is not the case at all. The regulations are being made under section 11 (1) (a) which says:
Notwithstanding any other provision in this division, the following amounts may-
And I leave out some words.
-be deducted in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year:
(a) Such part of the capital cost to the taxpayer of property, or such amount in respect of the capital costs to the taxpayer of property, if any, as is allowed by regulation.
I indicated in my budget speech last March the broad principles on which depreciation will be allowed. I agree with my friend that the rules with respect to depreciation are one of the most important aspects of income tax law because they vitally affect the profit of the taxpayer which is subject to tax. But it has never been considered possible to spell out in a statute the detailed rules with respect to depreciation. It has never been done. Under the old act it was left to the discretion of the minister. Under the new act we provide that it should be done by regulation; that is, that it should be formally enacted in specific terms, tabled in the house, published in the Canada Gazette and available for all who wanted to see it.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Afterwards, yes. But you have to have an effective order to make the regulations before you can enact the regulations. I have not seen these regulations yet. I understand that they are prepared and are ready for submission to cabinet council when this amendment is passed. My hon. friend quite properly asked me if I could let him

Income Tax Act
have them two or three days ago, and he referred to it today. I told him that I had not seen them myself. I have not seen them yet.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That does not impress me greatly. I am quite aware that under the clause in the statute these regulations can be made. But I am submitting to the minister, who is usually a reasonable man, that actually, without knowing a great deal more than we now know, we cannot give any intelligent consideration to this section 20 that is now before us. I know they are still tentative; nevertheless, they would have given us an understanding that we do not have at present. As it is now we are asked to approve these regulations really in the dark.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

I am not
quite through yet. Some of my colleagues are anxious to have a go at the minister and I will give way to them in just a moment. subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: We are told here up to the present, "incidentally, that the effect of this"-that is, of the new system- "will be to allow for obsolescence hitherto unrecognized under our act." subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am not a lawyer and therefore do not understand all the implications of this section, so I should like to present a specific case to the minister and ask him just

what happens in that case. A great many farmers, especially in western Canada, came under the income tax first between 1940 and 1943. We will take the case of a farmer who built, we will say, $10,000 worth of buildings in 1929 and in 1940 he comes under the income tax. He then writes off 5 per cent depreciation on the buildings, and that depreciation has been written off on the $10,000 that he started with. By 1949 his depreciation is all written off. He cannot take any further depreciation, although for five or ten years during the 1930's he was in the drought area or had no crop at all. He was paid P.F.A. Yet his right to take depreciation ceases at the end of twenty years. Is there any provision made for that? It seems unfair that he should not be able to take depreciation for twenty years during a period that he had not an actual income; it seems unfair that he should not be able to take depreciation on years when he had no income at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
If I understood my hon.
friend's case correctly, the farm that he referred to has been completely written off in the period to which he refers.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: As with all depreciation, you cannot take it twice.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, it was not written off. He never made income enough to write off any depreciation during maybe a five-year or ten-year period in the thirties. Prices were low or he had no crop. Yet the income tax people insist that by 1949 his right to depreciate those buildings has ceased. That seems unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I am told that is one of the reasons for making the change that is contemplated here. Under the old rules he had to take at least half the allowed depreciation in a particular year, whether he had profits or not. Under the new system he is not required to take any depreciation at all in the particular year unless he sees fit to do so, and obviously he will not do it unless he has profits against which the depreciation can be allotted.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That again brings up the difficulties under the act. Most farmers have not kept books. All the department has is their word that during that year they did not have an income. What proof will they have to give to the department that they did not have an income during any particular year in which they could not take depreciation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Of course if they had profits they took the full depreciation against the profits. Under the old rule they would be

obliged to, or they would be deemed to have taken half of the allotted depreciation whether profits existed or not. That has been operating up to the present time, and the result today would be that either the depreciation has actually been taken against the admitted profits or would have been deemed to have been taken to the extent of half the percentage allowed, applicable in each year in any case.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I have information, and it comes from a chartered accountant of considerable experience, that this is in fact a retrograde step. My information is that in the United Kingdom the practice is in accord with what is called the straight-line method of depreciation; whereas this amendment sets up the reducing balance system. Will the minister comment on that? If that is so, why are we changing to what has been described as an antiquated system?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I can only cite another
opinion. I have been informed by chartered accountants and others in whose judgment I have a good deal of confidence that this is not a retrograde step, but a step in advance and that it actually is better for the majority of taxpayers than the old system. I cannot be otherwise than assertive on that. That is the advice which I have received from my own advisers who are highly experienced in these matters. I can make no claim to being an expert myself. As I said before, this is a very technical subject, one in which the accountants are very much more expert than members of the legal profession. I can only rely on information which I receive that this is an improvement on our old system and essentially fairer to the taxpayer, and that is why we made the change.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: May I make two comments on that? The first one is that under this system the taxpayer can never entirely write off the asset, because it is a constantly reducing figure which is diminished each year, the suggestion being a straight 15 per cent of the initial cost. The second is, what is the practice in the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
On the first question my hon. friend is of course a highly skilled mathematician. He is quite right on the diminishing balance principle. You could not completely eliminate the value, but it can be reduced to infinitesimal proportions so that it ceases to have any commercial significance.
As to what the practice in the United Kingdom is, the information we have is that most of the British system is on the basis 45781-174J
Income Tax Act
which we are now adopting, but I am not prepared to assert that with absolute finality. That is the information we have.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I should like to get this down to fairly simple figures. Take the case of a farmer who has a tractor worth $5,000. At the end of five years that tractor has been fully written off. That farmer sells the tractor to another farmer for $2,000. Is the purchaser allowed to depreciate that $2,000, or has it been written off so far as he is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The new purchaser would depreciate it at the cost which is $2,000.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What about the farmer who sold it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He gets $2,000 back in income because he would have had the tax determined on a depreciated basis which has been proved in fact to be too great.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The farmer would receive $2,000 from the sale of his old tractor. He would buy a new tractor for $1,500 on which he would take depreciation, and he would have $500 to spare.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Which shows the great advantage of being a farmer.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: This is one section that will need almost an army to enforce. I am speaking now for the farmers. If it is properly understood it will arouse a degree of antagonism the like of which has never been known before. I come from a province where the farmers pay income tax. When they begin to realize the meaning of this change that my hon. friend passes off with that graciousness for which he is famous, it will take an army of employees to enforce it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Why does my hon. friend say that?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I say that simply for the reason that throughout the years in Saskatchewan the farmers have been in the position mentioned already by the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Acadia. They have brought before the committee a situation that is serious. This section makes no allowance for conditions that prevailed throughout the years. Suppose the machinery was purchased in 1932 or 1933 and there was no crop for five or six years and there was no depreciation during those years. If the farmer disposes of his machinery he finds himself in a position where he is subjected to further taxation. There will never be a closing of the farmer's liability for taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me, this applies only to depreciation from now on. I thought I made that clear in my initial statement. It does not relate to the past.

Income Tax Act

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I appreciate that. But when conditions are bad in any of the years, as they are for instance this year, then the situation is going to be most serious during any year that the farmer has a crop and disposes of any of his machinery that has been depreciated down. I suggest that the minister should give the widest publicity to this section and that the regulations should be published in all the papers. Some say that knowledge is strength. Knowledge of this section in the farming communities will arouse a great deal of ill feeling because it means that when a farmer has a crop after a series of no crops and disposes of any of the assets that have been depreciated down over five or six years, he will find himself paying an abnormal income tax on something that I personally regard as a serious invasion of his rights. I mention farmers particularly in that connection, for I believe that this section as now drafted will be productive of more antagonism than revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I have only one suggestion to make there. Perhaps I should not presume to suggest it but I think one should be careful about making assertions as to what the reaction will be-

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I have already received letters about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: -until the regulations are fully understood by those who will be affected by them. My hon. friend refers to bad years. Under the proposed new system, if the farmer to whom he alludes sells a piece of equipment at a loss he can continue to take depreciation on it, which he could never do before. He can average his profits over five years back and he can write a loss five years forwards and one year back. A combination of those various privileges I think will be found on application to be much more advantageous than the system which has prevailed up to the present time. Therefore I hope hon. members will not criticize the provisions in unqualified terms, until they are thoroughly informed as to the new regulations and the way they will work out.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is one good argument why the tentative regulations should be before the house so that, just as the hon. member for Greenwood has said, we may understand how these new changes are going to be applied. We make a general law in this section. I know one cannot cover a particular case in a general law; he must leave something to the matter of regulation. But those tentative regulations should be before the house so that hon. members may understand what the application will be in so far

as the taxing administration is concerned, in connection with the regulations about to be announced.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre that publicity should be given to this change, because I know it is a complete reversal of what has been happening in connection with depreciation on machinery. I know a great many farmers will not know anything about it unless some publicity is given to it; and they will continue to consider as capital gain the $1,000 or $500 for which they may sell a piece of equipment that has been depreciated, rather than place it in their income for taxation purposes, which has been the custom to date.
The minister has not answered my other question. He says the new legislation is not retroactive. Farmers during the thirties were not able to depreciate. There is depreciation taken on his buildings, whether he had an income in those years or not. That seems to be unfair.
The minister stated this new legislation will cover that, but it will not cover the retroactive period. That is the period they are worrying about-the time in the thirties when they were unable to take that depreciation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I wish I could explain a little more clearly than I have; however, I can only repeat what I said before, that this is probably the most complex and technical part of the income tax law. It is one which I think trained accountants are much better able to understand and explain than lawyers would be.
There will be no retroactive effect, so far as the new section is concerned. Value will be taken as it is today and depreciation will apply from now on. I sincerely believe, from the information I have been given, that they are more fair and more advantageous for the taxpayer than the rules which existed formerly. That is the only assurance I can give the house. I think we have to use the process of trial and error here as we do in so many other cases. These regulations to which I refer are still being worked on and will be put out as early as possible. I am informed by my officials who sit before me that the regulations, even if they were available today, might not help us in discussing the principle of the new rule. But, be that as it may, they are not yet ready.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Under the circumstances the minister should advise every farmer to have a chartered accountant make up his income tax next year. Farmers will not be able to

understand these regulations. Hon. members cannot get an explanation they can understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I am told however that the new system is simpler than the old one. So, I think it is like so many other cases-we are crossing our bridges before we get to them, and we are worrying about things we need not worry about. I would only ask the indulgence of the house to give this a fair trial. It would have been easy for us to have stuck to the old one. No one was complaining a great deal about it. I do not think one member in the house out of fifty really knew anything about it-and I include myself in the fifty. We are endeavouring to improve it. I apologize for not being able to explain it more clearly than perhaps others could do. However, that is the position.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is well for us to remember that this house, in legislating, while it has a responsibility with respect to the principle of the bill, also has a responsibility with respect to its form. Unless we can legislate in clear terms we are creating trouble for the taxpayer.
It is not without significance that when the minister sought to give the effect of the section he turned back to a speech he made on the budget last March. There he placed before us a paragraph which was clear and understandable. But when it gets down to a matter of carrying out the effect of the paragraph in the budget speech we find that there are in sections 7 and 8 of the bill, which are the sections dealing with depreciation, some six pages of legislative-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mostly definitions.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: -of legislative provisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mostly definitions.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Well, that does not subtract one iota from the difficulty of construing the sections.
I suppose there may have been times when taxing statutes enacted by parliament were clear and understandable, but it seems to me that time has gone by. If these sections are a fair example of the kind of legislation parliament is to be called upon to pass nowadays, then the days of clear legislation are gone. Looking over this bill, and seeing these sections, and subsections and clauses, and then the exceptions to the provisions, and the exceptions to the exceptions, and the provisos, and the provisos to the provisos, and so on scattered all through this bill, one wonders what on earth the result will be. It reminds me of an expression from an eminent
Income Tax Act
professor of the university of Toronto respecting the profound writings of Dean Roscoe Pound of Harvard law school on jurisprudence, when he said, "He uses English words, but it is not the English language."
One might say of these new provisions that they contain English words, but so far as we can find out they bear no resemblance to understandable English. It is very difficult for any man to follow them.
Then, there are a couple of points in particular I should like to mention. I understand it has been the practice in times past for the Department of National Revenue not to allow depreciation unless that depreciation is actually set up on the books of the taxpayer. That immediately raises the question as to the particular method of depreciation the taxpayer proposes to follow. I am informed that this reducing balance method as a basis of depreciation may become very cumbersome and unsatisfactory from the point of view of the taxpayer. If the taxpayer, to keep himself in the clear so far as the statute is concerned, is to follow this reducing balance method, and if, in trying to keep his books in such shape that he will understand them, he applies the straight line method, which is probably the one to which he has been accustomed, then he will be in great difficulty.
There are taxpayers who are urging upon the minister that the regulations be promulgated in the future so as to permit a choice of bases on the part of the taxpayer, and that he should be allowed to retain, if he so chooses, the straight line method.
There are several other features, and these have been drawn to the minister's attention. I refer particularly to a brief submitted to him by the board of trade of Toronto. These are matters with which it seems to me the minister has not dealt-or certainly has not dealt clearly tonight.
The first objection has to do with the retroactive feature. The minister has said there is no retroactive feature. I submit to him that it would be well if the new provision in respect of depreciation and the regulations yet to be made were made effective on a uniform date. It has been suggested that fiscal periods ending January 1, 1950, and subsequently would be satisfactory, and that the transitional provision could carry forward the former depreciation practice to that date.
The board of trade has made this comment:
It must be obvious that from an administrative point of -view this would be highly desirable. If this is not done, thousands of corporate statements already prepared and filed will be subject to amendment. Furthermore in a great many cases, where assets have been disposed of, a retroactive tax will

Income Tax Act
be imposed. The board believes that this is an improper manner of dealing with the tax-paying public, and strongly urges that this retroactive feature of the proposed law be not enacted.
It seems to me, in commenting upon that point, that that is good sense and clear logic.
The second point has to do with the effect of this provision upon the stranger who at some future date is making a purchase.
Paragraph (2) of section 20 deals with property passing between persons some of whom were not dealing at arm's length. The effect of the paragraph as drafted would seem to work a hardship against a bona fide stranger who is a final purchaser in a series of transactions one of which was not conducted at arm's length. This would obviously be unfair and the wording of the paragraph should be changed to avoid such a situation.
The point arises as to these definitions to which the minister has referred. The particular definition to which I am now about to allude is on page 6 under subsection 3 (c), the definition of "proceeds of disposition". You will observe that the third and fourth clauses of paragraph (c) include:
(iii)	an amount payable under a policy of insurance in respect of loss or destruction of property, and
(iv)	an amount payable under a policy of insurance in respect of damage to property except to the extent that the amount has, within a reasonable time after the damage, been expended on repairing the damage.
The submission of the board of trade on this point is:
Taken together these two items-
That is to say, paragraphs (iii) and (iv) which I have read.
-seem to mean that in case of a total loss by fire the insured company would be taxable on the proceeds of insurance to the extent that the proceeds exceeded the undepreciated capital cost, (but limited to the amount by which original capital cost exceeds undepreciated capital cost). In case of partial loss, no tax would arise if the proceeds of insurance were expended in repairing damage.
This could quite obviously work serious hardship in the case of total loss by fire. In such event part, and possibly a large part, of the insurance moneys would be required for taxes. It is quite possible that some companies would not be able to carry sufficient insurance to cover both the fire loss and the resulting tax, and therefore would not be able to replace the plant facilities.
Then the board proceeds to urge very strongly that the proviso in subparagraph 3 (c) (iv) regarding amounts expended to repair damage should be extended to 3 (c) (iii) to cover amounts expended on replacement. That seems to be a most sensible suggestion. Surely it would not be the wish of parliament that, where insurance is collected on what amounts to a total loss or nearly a total loss, the tax gatherer should step in then and treat the payment made by the insurance company as proceeds of disposition.
It seems to me these points illustrate the definite weaknesses and shortcomings in the
fMr. Fleming.]
legislation now before us. I would suggest that the two related sections, sections 7 and 8 of the bill, should be held over until the minister has had an opportunity to draft amendments that will overcome these very proper objections to the present wording.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I very carefully considered the representations from the Toronto board of trade to which my hon. friend has referred. As to the alleged retroactive question, I announced last March that depreciation for 1949 would be on the new basis. It is true the detailed regulations are not yet available, but I hope they will be within the next week or ten days. However, be that as it may, in the regulations it is proposed to insert a transitional provision that if the taxpayer takes depreciation in the year 1949 calculated on the old basis that dollar amount can be used for the 1949 period. In other words, he is given the option of taking it on that basis or on the new basis, whichever happens to be more advantageous. I think we have carefully guarded against any danger of retroactivity in the application of the new rules. I cannot agree with the submission of the board of trade on the question of insurance. If a man has insured a capital asset and he realizes an amount which is in excess of the written-down value he has in effect disposed of that asset, in an exceptional way it is true, and he has received a certain amount of cash for it. I see no reason why, if the proceeds of the insurance policy are in excess of the written-down book value, he should not be taxable on that excess.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Would it be all in the same year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He can of course refuse it and start depreciating on the new basis.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Does the minister think it is fair that that should all be taken in the one year? After all, if there was appreciation over a period of ten years, why should it all be taken and made taxable in the one year? Getting it down to the simple tractor from Acadia, where the farmer depreciated his tractor in five years, and at the end of that time showed $2,000 profit you would charge him all that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There is one thing which is not appreciated. Under the new system all assets are lumped together as a group. Under the old system each asset had to be valued on the books as a separate item and depreciated separately. Under the new system they are lumped together and all pooled, and your depreciation is against the pool. Therefore if he had two tractors one could be offset against the other. It is really writing back into the pool. Take the case of the ordinary

commercial enterprise where some stock in trade is lost as the result of a fire. Suppose it is not a total loss, but some machinery and equipment is lost, and there is other machinery and equipment and other assets which are depreciated. The collection on the insurance is $25,000 and the written down value is $20,000. Therefore there would be an apparent profit of $5,000 which would be taxable. That is taken into the operations for the year, but depreciation is taken against the pooled assets, and it is offset against that figure.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: How would the minister replace a saw mill if it was insured and then you came along and took your 20 per cent cut out of it? What has happened over the past seven or eight years is that costs have increased, and a saw mill that might have cost $500,000 then would cost $1 million to replace. Nevertheless, in the meantime you have reduced the capital you have there.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I believe the minister and the government are well aware that the taxation policy and agricultural policy in general have been responsible for the reduction in the production of agricultural products. I think that has been pointed out plainly many times in the house. Just as soon as farmers find out there is one more method by which their money can be filched away from them in the form of taxation, there will be a still greater reduction in the production of the country. I think it is a mistake to have the present system put into effect so far as farmers are concerned.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I find myself perplexed by the minister's attitude with regard to his refusal to admit that insurance money may be used for replacement as well as repairs. Let me ask, how much destruction must there be? In subparagraph 4 it says:
... in respect of damage to property except to the extent that the amount has, within a reasonable time after the damage, been expended on repairing the damage.
Suppose there is 95 per cent damage. Can he replace it? What if the whole thing is destroyed? Suppose there is 50 per cent damage; he can replace, but if the whole thing is destroyed then he is going to be taxed and he cannot use the money for replacing the building. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There are two separate things. The first paragraph, (iii), relates to loss or destruction, and the second one, (iv), relates to damage. In the case of loss or destruction the insured article is no longer there. It is not a case of repairing it but of replacing it. It is just as though the article has been
Income Tax Act
sold; the only thing is it has been sold to the insurance company instead of to a purchaser. So far as the taxpayer is concerned, he has the cash, and if he had sold it he would have to use the cash to replace it if he wanted to. Since it has been burned, or destroyed in some other way, he has the cash from the insurance company. If that amount of cash is greater than the written-down value of the asset, then in effect he has got back more than his capital; he has been claiming a deduction as a capital expense which in fact he has not incurred. Therefore on the recapture principle it should be subject to tax. If the asset is damaged the insurance money, if entirely used to repair the damage, will attract no tax; but if there is an excess over and above what is required for repair then I take it that would be taxable income.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I understand the recapture principle; in fact that is the only thing I have understood tonight, really. It still seems to me that you are running into an absolutely illogical and even fantastic situation if you say the man whose building is ninety-five per cent ruined can replace or restore the damage, while the man whose building is one hundred per cent ruined cannot do so. Let us be frank about this. Insurance very seldom covers the whole value of a building, as we all know. In the practical outcome of this, say a man has a building worth half a million dollars, and he gets $400,000. According to the statement just made by the minister he can still be taxed on part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, there would be no tax at all under those conditions. If the written-down value of his buildings is half a million dollars and he collects only $400,000 in insurance, he has had a loss. The new system would help him get the $100,000 back, because he can include that loss of $100,000 in his general pool. He could not have included a capital loss of that kind before; but if you have a running capital account of this kind you can take capital losses into it. That is one of the advantageous features of the new principle.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Toronto board of trade stated a simple case, and I thought it was put very sensibly. Let me read it again, to see where the defect may be: The board draws your attention to paragraph (3) subsections (c) (iii) and (c) (iv) which define "proceeds of disposition" to include proceeds of insurance policies. Taken together these two items seem to mean that in case of a total loss by fire the insured company would be taxable on the proceeds of insurance to the extent that the proceeds exceeded the undepreciated capital cost (but limited

Income Tax Act
to the amount by which original capital cost exceeds undepreciated capital cost). In case of partial loss, no tax would arise if the proceeds of insurance were expended in repairing the damage.
It seems to me the point is that in the case of partial loss the provision is sensible, but if you have the other case you run into this tax, which could prevent a man from carrying on his business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: My hon. friend cited the case of a ninety-five per cent loss. If the proceeds were used to repair the loss there would be no tax. If on the other hand the proceeds from the insurance were $10,000 and it cost $9,000 to repair the ninety-five per cent loss, the extra $1,000 would be taxable.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Numbers of people in my constituency own timber, on which in some cases they have paid taxes for from twenty to thirty or forty years, and they have also spent money developing and caring for it. Many of these people sell their timber on a stumpage basis for poles, logs, and so on. Are the receipts from that depreciated capital taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I am told that if the timber is sold on a stumpage basis the proceeds are taxable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: As a farmer I am just a little alarmed about this provision. We have become accustomed to the present method of depreciation of farm equipment and farm buildings, and now I want to ask the minister this question. In what way does this section alter the present method of calculating depreciation on farm buildings and equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I would like to give my hon. friend a detailed answer, but I am afraid I cannot do so. I am informed by people who are versed in this rather intricate subject of depreciation that the farmer will be better off under the new system than he was under the old one. I am making that as an assertion. I may be wrong, but I do not think I am, because we did not have to change the old system but did so in order to improve it. I return to what I said a little earlier. I wish I were technically competent to explain the intricacies of this matter, but I am not. However, I am assured by people who have made a study of it that it is an improvement on the old system and that it is better for the taxpayer, which includes the farmer as well as anyone else. That is why we have brought it in. I am afraid I cannot point out just why that should be so, though I shall try to in any specific instances that may be mentioned, but I suggest that people should not get too alarmed about the adverse effects of this provision before they see how it works out.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The more I hear the minister attempt to explain this section the more amazed I become that anyone would contemplate applying this to the farmers of Canada. A moment ago the minister said that in his opinion it would be simpler and easier for people to work out, but in view of what he went on to say I do not see how that can possibly be the case. In the past practically every farmer I have known has had considerable difficulty computing his income tax. Many of them have had to get help from a chartered accountant, or someone of that sort. It seems to me that by putting through this section we will force every farmer to obtain the services of a chartered accountant; and as a result you are going to encounter intense opposition on the part of the farming population to this method of income tax assessment, as far as depreciation is concerned.
Under the old system when a farmer bought a new article, whether it was a tractor, a binder, a combine or anything else, all he had to do was take the cost and move the decimal point over, or in other words divide it by ten. If it was an ordinary piece of farm equipment it was on a ten-year depreciation basis, and the farmer could put down that figure one year after the other. If it was on a twenty-year basis he multiplied by two; if it was on a five-year basis he divided by two, and that was all there was to it. Even that was difficult enough for most people to follow through with many pieces of farm equipment. Now the basis has been changed, as I understand it. If a man buys a piece of equipment for $1,000, we will say, he depreciates it 15 per cent the first year, which brings it down to $850. The next year he has to depreciate it another 15 per cent of that amount. So the farmer is going to have to wrack his brains and spend goodness knows how long trying to figure it out. He will have to take each item separately year after year, and he just will not do it. He does not have time; he will not be bothered with it, and as a result you will not collect your taxes. In other words if you put through this amendment I should say you may get a farmers' strike as far as income tax is concerned. They will not be bothered with it and will not do it. I think you are simply laying yourselves open to all kinds of trouble. It would be much better to leave the old system, under which a man knew how to calculate his depreciation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: As my hon. friend realizes, this is intended to be a relieving section; and it is.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It is intended to give the taxpayer further relief. Admittedly there may be a little difficulty getting it started, in arriving at initial values, but I am told when

that has been done it is very much simpler to calculate depreciation than under the old system. I am making that as an assertion, relying upon the advice of people in whose experience I have some confidence. While I know some people are always averse to change and always think the present system is the best in the best possible world, that is not my philosophy. In matters of depreciation as in other matters I think we may be able to bring about an improvement. No farmer is obliged to take depreciation; it is an advantage which enables him to reduce the amount of his tax. Again I appeal for a fair trial for this new basis, which I am assured is better and simpler than the old one.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The thing I think will be in the minds of most hon. members is this: If the minister does not quite understand the implication of this section, I do not know how he expects the farmers to do so. As a matter of fact, I have heard some members of this committee say that the farmer would likely have to have an accountant make out these forms. He has to have an accountant now. I do not suppose there are many farmers, certainly not in my part of the country, who make out their income tax forms themselves. Instead of making these forms more complicated, instead of making the law so obscure that even the minister is not able to understand it, I believe we should be simplifying it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I did not say that. I said it was a little difficult to explain in generalities.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: If a thing is difficult to explain, perhaps the person who is explaining it does not understand it himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Or his audience; but that is the fault of the minister, not his audience.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
So far as the income tax which is applicable to agriculture is concerned, I have always felt, and I believe it is the thought of most people representing agricultural sections, that the call is constantly for some sort of simplification in the tax structure. The farmer does not want to have to go to his lawyer or accountant, and spend days getting his income tax in shape. The farmer is in an entirely different position from the ordinary individual. You cannot put his business on the same level as the ordinary business of industry and commerce. There is a distinction between the two.
All the minister has to do is to look casually into the distinction between the way a farmer has to conduct his business, and the way the business of industry is conducted. In most instances, there is little in common. When it comes to making out income tax
Income Tax Act
returns, however, both of them are put in the same box, and are asked to make out their income tax returns on the same basis. This has been the difficulty facing agriculture during these last few months. There has been a great deal of agitation over the complex nature of the returns the farmer is asked to make out. Upon completion of the return, the farmer is never sure whether he owes the government $10 or $1,000. I believe once the farmer sees this act, he will have great difficulty in coming to the conclusion that he can make out his income tax return.
If we are going to make a move in any direction, I plead with the minister to make a move towards a simpler sort of return for agriculture, having in mind the fact that agriculture is in an entirely different position from industry. Apparently, industry is the section of our population upon which the income tax return standards are based. I wonder what industry would think if the farmers were to have the say as to what kind of income tax return there should be in this country? Industry would raise a howl to the high heavens, but a farmer is expected to fit himself into the sort of strait-jacket that has been prepared for industrial income tax returns. I believe the minister ought to consider that whole question, to ascertain whether we cannot have a simpler form for agriculture, because it is working a great hardship upon farmers generally from one end of Canada to the other.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It was both comforting and challenging to hear the Minister of Finance say a few moments ago that he was technically unable to explain this section, or that he had not the technical knowledge or ability to explain the section. Now, that may be quite comforting to the rest of us who have tried to understand-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Not the section, if my learned friend will allow me, but the detailed way in which this new system operates. The section is largely a section of definitions.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
-how it is to be worked out in the legislation now proposed. We are being asked to put into effect provisions which many of the members of this house, if they find themselves in the same position as the minister, will not understand when they are called upon to vote on them.
There is a great deal more than depreciation involved in this provision. If it were simply the changing from one method of depreciation to another, the matter would not offer nearly the complexity or difficulty that it does. It goes beyond that. It is a method of depreciation accompanied by a capital gains tax; in effect, that is what it is.

Income Tax Act
If this were a perfectly sound method of depreciation, this new method of the reducing balance instead of the straight-line method hitherto in effect, surely it should commend itself to the department. The department would say, "Very well, as a method of depreciation we are satisfied with the soundness of the reducing balance method and will accept it". The department does not do that. They say that when a sale is made of a depreciated asset later on they are going to step in and take what amounts, in effect, to a capital levy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Chairman, it means just that. You take a simple transaction. John Jones buys something and sells it. If he is not in the business of buying and selling things of that class, then whatever he has made on that transaction is a capital gain, and is not income. Therefore, it is not subject to income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: If he did not claim depreciation, my hon. friend would be quite right.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
If the depreciation method that is proposed is sound, why should it not stand simply as a matter of depreciation? In this provision, the department is proposing to follow the asset, and it may go through more than two hands. If at some time in the future you are selling it at a greater value than the reduced value at which you are carrying it on your books, the department is going to treat that excess over the reduced value as income upon which you will be taxed. This will mean that the taxpayer is going to be pushed into a much higher bracket carrying a much higher rate of tax. It seems to me that that, sir, is the effect of this section. It is not simply a depreciation section, but is a section that provides for a method of depreciation and then goes much farther. It provides for the levying of a tax in a way that seems to me to amount to a capital gains tax.
Quite apart from that, sir, there are two points with which the minister has not dealt. In the first place, I raised a point as to the effective date, and the minister has indicated that regulations will make it possible for the taxpayer to make his choice between the two methods of depreciation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: On the amount for a whole year.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
For fiscal periods, yes, up until January 1, 1956. Beyond that time there will not be a choice, but during this period there will be a choice. I should like to ask the minister, if he will, to clear up this

point. It is tied up always with the requirement that the department insists that the depreciation must be set up in the books, and in the case of this option, the department will presumably insist on applying the method that the taxpayer has set up on his books.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That will be covered by the regulations, I understand. I understand that the practice in the Department of National Revenue in the past has been that depreciation claimed for tax purposes must be the depreciation which is actually set up on the books. Now, the regulations to be enacted will cover that point, as well as provide some modification in the rule, perhaps. I am informed that has not been settled yet.
I should like to revert for a moment to what my friend has said. I think the fundamental principle here is fairly clear, as to the basis upon which the taxpayer is entitled to recover his capital, because that is the purpose of depreciation and obsolescence allowances. The detailed method as to how it is done is to be made the subject of regulations. The only reason that these sections are complex, and the regulations are rather lengthy, is that, in accordance with what seems to be the general wish of the members of this house and the public, we have eliminated the old ministerial discretion. Under the old system there were no long, elaborate regulations published and available for anybody. You went to the minister. There were certain predetermined rates of depreciation. You went to the minister and he had to rule upon the matter and he did not bother to have that spelled out in a section or to enact regulations. It was a ministerial discretion, exercised no doubt, in all cases, fairly and so on and so forth. But inevitably, in getting away from that we have had to draw rather long and complex regulations.
But the principle of the proposed new system is as simple as a, b, c. The application is quite complicated, it is true, but this recapture provision which has been referred to has been followed in England where the principle of capital gains does not apply. The principle is simply this. If you start off with a cost, you would depreciate that cost on a diminishing balance basis, each year, at the predetermined rate and take your depreciation for your book value at the beginning of the year. Obviously in mathematics you will never write it off completely. You will get down to a fraction of a cent. The recapture provision is simply this. If you sell it for more than the depreciated cost, you have more depreciation deducted from your tax bill than you should have

had, and you should bring the difference back into your tax. It is just as simple as that. The application in different types of assets is admittedly complicated, and in talking in general terms it is difficult to explain particular cases. But there is nothing obscure about the main principle. Even a simple lawyer like myself can understand it.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: My point was not cleared up, Mr. Chairman. I am coming back to this point about the method of depreciation set up on the books of the taxpayer in 1949. This is the fifth day of December and when this bill becomes law, either the taxpayer is going to have an opportunity of sitting down then and deciding which of the two methods he chooses to apply for 1949 or the department is going to say: We have looked at your books and we find that this is the method you have been following; therefore because of the rule that the department allows depreciation only where it is set up on the books of the company or the taxpayer, we are going to apply that method. I am wondering how much time the taxpayer is going to have to exercise this option as between the two methods of depreciation for 1949.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, very few taxpayers with complicated accounts are actually in a position to close their accounts and make their final entries until some time after the end of the fiscal period. That is why this three months, or it is six months now, is allowed for filing the income tax return. With the demand for accountants and auditors, it is seldom that you can get your audited statement until some little time after the end of your fiscal year. I am informed that it should be possible to have the new regulations available before the end of the year. I realize that is only three weeks away, nevertheless the Department of National Revenue are hopeful that as soon as this legislation is adopted they will be able to complete the regulations and publish them. While the time may be somewhat short, nevertheless I think there really will be adequate time for those who have to look at one option or the other to see which it would be in their interests to follow.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: My point has not been answered.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The hon. member for Acadia.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
When the minister argues that the new scheme will be fairly simple or that it will be just, I am not going to take exception to that remark. But on the other hand, when he says that the farmer will be better off under this system, then I say that he is
Income Tax Act
just talking poppycock, because it will cost the farmer more money. It is bound to cost him more money. Let me explain what I mean. At the present time it is quite common practice for large farmers to sell off their machinery about every fourth or fifth year because they do not want to run the risk of delay at seeding time or harvest time. Seeding time and harvest time are short periods and they do not want to take the chance of a breakdown. So they make it a practice to sell off their machinery about every four or five years and buy new machinery. In the past, when they have sold off their old machinery, they have not had to pay any income tax on the price they received for it. But now the minister says they will have to pay a tax. How can the farmer possibly be better off when he now has to pay a tax which he has not had to pay in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: They would not have to pay tax unless they sold the machinery at an amount greater than the depreciated value.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is what I am talking
about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Are the farmers making a great deal of money selling second-hand machinery?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is not the purpose of selling the machinery. The purpose is to avoid loss of time as a result of using the old machines at harvest time or seeding time. The farmer might easily lose the price of a machine or half the price of a machine. But if the machine has been fully depreciated, he is going to have to pay income tax on the sale price. That has not been the practice in the past. Whether or not it is just is a question I am not going to argue. But the impression now is that he is going to have to pay a tax now that he has never had to pay in the past, and it will not be popular. The minister cannot argue that it is going to be popular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The farmer must be selling it to another farmer who would buy the same sort of machine.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: They are going to the dealer for new machines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I see. I am asking for information. Where does the old machine go?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The dealer sells it to another farmer. He reconditions it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Order. May I ask hon. members to address themselves to the Chair.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The dealer reconditions the machine and sells it to another farmer, and the other farmer will be allowed depreciation on that machine. But in the past, the farmer

Income Tax Act
who has turned that machine in to the dealer has never had to pay income tax on the amount he received for the machine; but from now on he will have to do so. As I say, that is not going to be popular at all; in fact it is going to be exceedingly unpopular. I assure the minister that he will find that out as soon as the farmers begin to realize that they are going to have to pay that tax.
There is one other point I wish to mention. At the present time any expenditure of over $25 on capital has to be considered a capital investment and cannot be charged as an expenditure; that is if the amount is over $25. We find that farmers sometimes get wells drilled and spend perhaps $600. They do not strike any water. It is a dry hole. But they are not allowed to charge for that expenditure. They have to charge it as a capital investment. How much of an investment have you got when you have a dry hole? Yet they have to depreciate that dry well for ten years. It seems to me that that is nonsensical. Where a farmer goes to the expense of getting a well drilled, spends $600 on that well and gets no water, then he should be allowed to charge that as an expenditure for that year, because he must make a capital expenditure to get another well drilled in order to get water. It seems to me that provision is most unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: May I give my hon. friend a specific illustration of how this works with respect to a machine, for instance, because that seems to be the case which is causing some concern. Suppose he sells a particular type of farm machinery for $4,500. Suppose that represents $500 over and above the depreciated value of that machine, so that he would appear to have a profit of $500. Then suppose at the same time he buys a new machine for $5,000. He sets off the $500 against the $5,000 price for his new machine, and the cost of his new machine to start depreciating from is $4,500, so that he pays no tax on what would seem for the moment to be a $500 profit. This is a continuing operation. That is the way in which what I probably not too accurately referred to as the pool system of depreciation works in the case of a farmer or any other taxpayer. There would be no tax payable on the $500 as a profit. That is the point I am making in the illustration I have given. It would be used to write down the value of the new machine which he bought in its place. He does not take it into income.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Has the minister or his department consulted any farm organization with respect to this change in depreciation before writing the act? Will they consult with

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, back in 1947 the department got out a farmer's income tax guide. Last year there was not one published. I wonder whether-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: There was.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

speechtext: All the discussion that has been going on here tonight?

speechtext:
I want to return to this
question of tax on timber entirely liquidated. I want to give the minister one example that illustrates the point. I know of people who have held timber for forty years, owning the land and the timber. They paid taxes for forty years and cared for it. Theoretically

a man could sell that timber off the stump in one year and obtain $20,000 or $25,000, and in doing so he would in reality completely liquidate his capital. After he conserves that timber all throughout these years he is taxed on the total receipts. I ask the minister how he can justify that tax on capital depreciation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Well, of course, if he sold the land with the timber on it, that would be a sale of capital asset. If he did as my hon. friend suggested, sold it on a stumpage basis in one year he could be taxed on the receipts in one year, on his income less any expense he incurred. Presumably in the thirty or forty years that he has held the land he has deducted his expenses of carrying it as a deduction from income. I would assume that in these circumstances the taxpayer would endeavour to dispose of the land on such a basis over a period of time that it would not attract taxes in a single year. subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Can the minister say where that is in the section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not in the section. The principle is found in section 11, subsection 1, which says that the taxpayer is entitled to recover his capital in accordance with regulations to be determined by the minister. Under the old act it was discretionary. It was not in the act at all. It was discretionary. Now it is going to be spelled out in regulations. But the principle which underlies depreciation or obsolescence or depletion is that you are entitled to take as an expense an item representing the day by day, the month by month return of your capital through age, wear or use, and the principle is that you should not be taxed on income before you get your capital, at least that you should get your capital back, and that it is not true income so long as a portion of what you are receiving is a return of capital. subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I know the minister wants to be fair, but he has been a little bit dense about getting this machinery through. Nevertheless he has been fair. He has been trying to block up the holes in taxation. He says if a man bought a machine at $1,000 and depreciated it over a period of five years the machine is gone. Then if he turns around and buys a new one and gets credit of $500 on the old one he starts off with what he got on the other machine.
I come from an agricultural district and I am sure that the minister wants to be fair to all farmers. If a corporation or a man is in business and saves $100,000 he can go to the taxation branch and if he is the manager of that business he can get a fairly good compensation for being the manager of the business. Farmers are managers of their businesses, but I cannot see any section in this act which says that farmers are entitled to any compensation for being managers. There are thousands of farmers in western Canada who should be entitled to management compensation just the same as other people in business. I hope that when the minister looks at this in a fair way he will give them consideration.
The hon. member for Acadia spoke about farmers drilling for water and after having been put to considerable expense found that there was no water there and were not entitled to any consideration. I would ask the minister to give the same consideration to the farmers as he has to those who, under section 52, are exploring and drilling for oil. If he does that it will be quite fair.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Would the minister reply to the point I raised about the well? When I asked my question he was busy arguing on the other matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Would the hon. member repeat his question. I know it has been up before in the previous debate, so perhaps he would ask it again.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Under the ruling of the income tax branch, if a farmer spends more than $25 on capital development he cannot show that as current expenditure. He must show it as capital investment. We will suppose a farmer drills a well at a cost of $600, and does not strike water. It is not an asset; but he is not allowed to show it as a current expenditure, and has to allow depreciation on it over a period of ten years. How can you depreciate something that does not exist? You have not got the well. He will have to drill another well, and when he drills that well it will be carried for ten years. But surely the well he drilled from which he got no water should be allowed as a current expenditure in that year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I shall have to discuss the matter. It is in the Department of National Revenue, and I do not know what the practice has been there. If a farmer spent $500 looking for water, and did not get the water, he would not have any asset to write off. He has just made an expense, for which he has no return. If he spent $500 and actually got a well, then he would have a capital asset. But that is not one which depreciates. Presumably, so long as nature continues to function, the well will continue as an asset, in perpetuity. He does not have to get back the capital, because his capital is undestructible.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, not in respect of a well. He would be lucky if he had a well which would last more than ten years. At the end of ten years he would probably have to put in a new casing or have to drill a new well. But my argument is that when you do not get water you should be allowed to show it as an expense, and it should be exempt for the full amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I shall talk on that with the Minister of National Revenue. I can see some objection to allowing it as a current expense in the year in which it is incurred.

"Total depreciation allowed to a taxpayer"_

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
We are talking about a gain. I say therefore that there is a very pronounced change made here, and that so far as the farmer is concerned-and I am using him only as an example of all classes -it means that farmers throughout the country will find themselves in a position where they will be taxed on what in effect heretofore has been a capital gain. This affects Saskatchewan particularly, because Saskatchewan is one province in which the farmers pay tremendous income tax.
That is what it amounts to. I am not for one moment dealing with the question of losses. This in effect is the first time parliament has made a provision for the taxation of capital gain, and this may well be the thin edge of the wedge in that direction. That is why it deserves consideration. While the minister says that all we do is to make some minor change, in effect by these provisions we are altering our system of taxation and, as regards the example I have brought to the attention of the committee, we are placing a tax upon what heretofore has been a capital gain.
The minister has said, "Do not prejudge us." I say if the farmers of western Canada had known what he meant when he read the statement upon the introduction of his budget last spring, and which he re-read this evening, there would have been an altogether different reaction toward this matter.
This is a change which cannot but arouse antagonism, for it is a change in the system of taxation, and will mean a larger amount of taxation payable by the people of this country who are affected by this provision.
The expression the minister used is that it is a recapture. It is more than a recapture; it is the first capture of a capital gain in this country. It is for that reason I suggest it be held in abeyance and not brought into effect. It is not just simply a method of altering the system of depreciation. It is in effect a form of additional taxation, and one that merits the consideration of members on all sides of the house. It is a change. It is all very well to say that losses may also be subtracted, but in so far as gains are concerned it is a capital gains tax.
