subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I come back to the subject of the capital tax which I mentioned some little while ago. It seems to me that the Department of National Revenue must initially take the responsibility for saying what is a reasonable rate of depreciation, one that they will allow. Having done that, surely it is only reasonable that the department should stay with that rate of depreciation. If the taxpayer later on sells the depreciated article for more than the written-down value on his books, then why on earth should the tax-gatherer step in and lay his hands upon the excess? It comes back to this, that the department is saying that they allowed too much depreciation.
In the first place it seems to me it is the responsibility of the department to set such a rate of depreciation as will be fair. Having set that and enforced it for whatever period of time is in question, surely they should be satisfied to leave it at that. What is involved here is a great deal more than that. The government is not contenting itself with saying: We are going to set up a new method

of depreciation. The Department of National Revenue is not going to content itself with simply setting a rate of depreciation. If they guess low then they are going to follow the asset when sold, and lay their hands on what is a capital gain. The hon. member for Lake Centre is perfectly right in saying this represents the first time parliament has undertaken to tax a capital gain.
When I mentioned this matter earlier this evening I gave a simple illustration. John Jones buys an article and he sells it at a profit. In effect that is a capital gain. He is not taxable on it unless he is in the business of buying and selling articles of that class. The minister says: Oh, well, the difference here is that you are introducing depreciation. Let them introduce their depreciation, but let them stop at depreciation. They set the rate, and if they do not set it at a proper figure, then surely the proper course for them to follow is to set a proper and reasonable rate. Let them revise their rate, and not follow the asset when sold and tax a capital gain. It is a vicious principle, and one that has never been recognized by parliament before. As has been mentioned here, it is going to affect farmers. Actually, it is going to affect every taxpayer in Canada into whose calculation of income depreciation enters in any form, because the moment that he sets up depreciation he has invited a capital gains tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I have one observation. I do not want to hold up the committee, but one of the things we have been urged most strongly to make provision for is obsolescence, which has never been allowed before. I know of no way in which one can make provision for obsolescence except by setting maximum annual rates of depreciation which cannot be other than arbitrary, and can only represent an intelligent guess as to what will be the depreciation or obsolescence in that year, and if those expectations are not realized either take the excess back into profit or allow less to be charged. This is not a capital gains tax. It is the system which has been followed under the income tax provisions of the United Kingdom where capital gains have never been taxed, in the same way that they have never been taxed here. One of the things we are trying to accomplish by the changed system is to allow for obsolescence. This is the only way that I can see in which it can be done.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I should like to place another example before the minister and ask him what he thinks about it. We will say I invest $5,000 in a house, write off 5 per cent depreciation for ten years, and then sell the house for more than I paid for it. That is a capital gain, and I do not pay any tax on

the amount. On the other hand, if I invest $5,000 in a piece of farm equipment, the price of farm equipment rises over the years, and I then sell that piece of farm equipment, you say it is not a capital gain and that it is taxable. I think the same rule should apply in both cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It does apply in both cases if depreciation is taken on the house. As my hon. friend knows, one cannot claim depreciation as an expense on the house in which one lives. If it is a rented house you can claim depreciation at whatever the attributed rates are, 5 per cent or li. per cent. We will say the depreciated value of the house is $6,000, written down from $9,000, and that it is sold for $7,000. In effect it will have been overdepreciated, and there will have been a greater amount claimed as a deduction from income than should have been claimed. The $1,000 will go back in. In most cases it does not apply to private residences; it applies to machinery, equipment, business premises, and that sort of thing.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I wonder if the minister can explain to us what the situation will be as to farm buildings under the new system so far as depreciation is concerned. Let me take a specific example. We will say a farm is purchased for $20,000. The buildings on the farm cost the original owner $10,000 to erect. He has depreciated them until their value, so far as he is concerned with the income tax people, is $500. The man who buys the farm figures the buildings are worth $5,000, and he estimates that of the $20,000 he paid for the farm $15,000 was for the land and $5,000 for the buildings. What is his situation under the new system so far as depreciation on the buildings is concerned? Does he have to put them in at $500, does he put them in at the $5,000 he figures they are worth to him, or does he put them in at replacement cost which at present prices would be $10,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I would think the figure he would put them in at would be the portion of the price which he has paid that can be reasonably attributed to the value of the buildings. That would be the fair value of these buildings. My hon. friend gave an example of $20,000 for the land and the buildings. The fair value for the buildings would be $5,000. He would put those in at $5,000 and depreciate on that figure. The rest would be land, of course, which does not depreciate, so he would not claim anything there.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The minister says he thinks that would be the case. Does he know?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The matter of the fair attributable value would be a question of fact. If there were a dispute between the taxpayer
Income Tax Act
and the income tax department it would be settled by agreement or by the income tax appeal board and then on to the exchequer court; but the question as to the proportion of the price fairly attributable to the buildings as distinct from the land would be a question of fact.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It has nothing to do with the depreciated value?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The minister is completely wrong with respect to provinces where they have the Torrens system of land holding. In that case the registrar of the particular district in which the lands were situated just would not pay any attention to the principle you are talking about. The provincial tax would be on the value of the buildings at the time they were purchased, so the man in that case would be soaked both ways. Under your scheme he might pay very little but in provincial taxes he would pay a tremendous amount, because the actual or replacement cost of these buildings would be taken at so much and the land at so much. So you are going contrary to the established practice where the Torrens system applies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I suppose that is a provincial tax on the transfer, the land and building value?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: My suggestion is that the value the new purchaser would place on the buildings for purposes of depreciation would be the fair portion of the purchase price he paid which would be attributable to those buildings.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I had forgotten the name of it, but now I remember it is called the assurance fund. In all provinces where the Torrens system applies they have something called an assurance fund, which is in direct contradistinction to the principle we are discussing now. So a purchaser would pay in perhaps two ways, under the law in a province where the Torrens system applies and under the system the minister is describing. I am quite sure many difficulties will arise. Knowing the minister, I am sure he will get his share, and the province will be called the blood sucker in the picture. The individual will suffer, whatever name he is called.

speechtext: As the result of a letter which I received since we started to discuss this matter I should like to ask the minister for a ruling. I am sure that the house is glad to see the changes that are being made in connection with the definition of allowable medical expenses. I should like to raise again the two subjects that I have raised several times in previous sessions in connection with this matter of allowable medical expenses.
The first concerns eyeglasses. Parliament has made provision for the allowance of the cost of aids to hearing as a deductible medical expense; that provision has existed for several years. We are now allowing aids to those who are crippled, artificial limbs and wheel chairs. I contend there is no distinction in principle between an aid to hearing and an aid to seeing. Nevertheless, as the law is administered today, the department will allow the cost of an aid to hearing, but will not allow the cost of aids to seeing. It seems to me that is an altogether illogical and unfair stand. The matter has been before the minister, and I would urge that before parliament meets again, he give the subject favourable consideration, and submit amendments which will permit those who have to make outlays for aids to seeing to deduct those as medical expenses.
The other point has to do with the purchase of drugs and medicines. Everyone knows quite well the discrimination which exists against city residents in this respect. When a physician prescribes drugs or medicines, fills the prescription himself and includes the cost of the drug or medicine in his account,
Income Tax Act
the department admits it as a medical expense. If, as is the custom in urban centres, the physician simply writes a prescription which the taxpayer takes to the pharmacist, who fills the prescription, and charges separately for it, regardless of how much the taxpayer may have to spend on the necessary medicines and drugs, he is not permitted to have one cent deducted as medical expenses. Again that seems to me illogical and thoroughly unfair. It seems to me that situation has been allowed to continue quite long enough. I urge the minister to submit amendments at the earliest opportunity at the next session which will eliminate that unfair feature.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: In order to illustrate to the minister what I have in mind, I would recall to him the religious order known as the Hutterites. I believe that they pay income taxes. I think I am quite safe in saying that they do pay income tax on the total income of that colony or religious community.

In addition, sir, I think you will find that the community itself does pay a lump-sum tax on the total of the community income. I administered that regulation for the Alberta government for some years before you took it over, sir, and I understand that you do the same thing. These Hutterite colonies are now within the definition the minister has given of religious communities or orders. It is for that reason they organize themselves as they do. Every member has taken what amounts to a vow of perpetual poverty, because not one of them draws anything more than his board and bed.
What I want to point out is this. Will the Hutterite colonies have to be told by anybody that, if they just change their procedure a little bit, and at the end of the year apportion to each member of the community his share of the year's increase and then say simply, in accordance with your vows of perpetual poverty, you give it back to the community, they can bring themselves within the provisions of this subsection, and apply for exemption from taxation? I just wanted to point that out to the minister.
One other thing: I believe the minister will find that certain Doukhobor colonies across this country are organized on a similar basis. I believe there are other religious communities, and I know of one in particular, in which the members have gone so far as to take a vow of perpetual poverty. They have concentrated not only all their money, but I believe would even give their life for their religious community. Under such circumstances, they might, by a slight change in their procedure, come within the terms of this section and claim exemption from taxation.

speechtext:
I am appealing to the minister that, after all the refusals he has given us, he should now let us have a crumb from the table. I want to read to him quite briefly what he said in his budget speech last March. In announcing the section which it is now sought to repeal, he said this, as reported at page 1798 of Hansard:
At present we have a flat rate of 30 per cent on. all corporate profits. I am recommending that this 30

per cent be reduced to 10 per cent on profits up to $10,000 and increased to 33 per cent on profits in excess of $10,000. The house will at once recognize this as tax relief for small businesses and will, I trust, be heartily in accord with the policy.
I think the house was. We in this party-had advocated the very same thing and we were naturally in full accord. The minister continued:
Our country as a whole owes a great deal to the small family type of business. They have to struggle along, grow and develop in competition with large and well-financed corporations whose activities may be nation-wide. My own belief is that small businesses should be encouraged and it seems to me that a useful way to do this is to lower the tax and take less out of the funds they need for growth and expansion.
I call your attention to this, Mr. Chairman, the minister continued:
All corporations, regardless of size, will, of course, receive this relief on the first $10,000 of profits but, as I have said, the rate of tax on profits in excess of this figure will bfe increased by 3 per cent.
Now we have this amendment changing what was then contemplated, what we had welcomed and what I still think was a wise provision. I understand the reason for the change. As always happens, there are certain people trying to take an improper advantage to which they are not entitled; but I am still confident that the minister and his staff can, as I said in the other case, prevent improper advantage being taken of it. I think it will be a most unfortunate thing if this section is watered down to the point where it will be of little value. The provision as now introduced, whereby related companies will be regarded as if they were only one company, and only one of the related companies will have this $10,000 provision, is, I submit, going to destroy the effect of the section. I hope that the minister will be prepared, as I say, to exercise his ingenuity and that of his staff to prevent invasions of it and to preserve this highly beneficial provision which we were just on the point of getting. In other words, I hope that it will not be still-born.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This is a section to which we have been giving a good deal of care and thought. From the very outset we realized that we would have to insert in the act a provision to prevent the splitting up of large companies in order to take advantage of the 10 per cent rate. For instance, a chain store could incorporate all its stores as separate entities and get the benefit.
At the very outset, when I made my budget speech in March, we contemplated that the legislation would contain an appropriate provision with respect to related companies. Possibly the section which is contained in this bill is a bit more rigid than it needs to be;
Income Tax Act
I am not prepared to say that it is and I am not prepared to say that it is not. Over the last two or three months I have received many representations, and some highly constructive ones too, from various taxpayers. Certain suggestions have been made. The principal one was that we should consider those companies which were created prior to the adoption of the act as one group and not apply this rule to them. But that does not commend itself to me, and I am glad to see that the hon. member for Greenwood shakes his head.
It is an important question. It is a new thing; it is a new departure. It has never been tried either here or in any other country before. I finally came to the conclusion that, before I make a definite change, I want more time to consider the possible alternatives. Two or three have been suggested. I have not been able to convince myself that any one of them is the proper one. But the undertaking I would give to the committee is this. Between now and the time we introduce the 1950 budget I will see if we can work out a more satisfactory section. Since 1949 is the first year that the section will operate, there can be no objection to making any amendment which it was decided was desirable apply to the 1949 period. In other words, I should like to leave the question open for another two or three months in order to enable me and my officials to see if we can arrive at some more satisfactory solution, if one can be found. I readily give that undertaking. I have a completely open mind on the matter. I hope we may be able to find an amendment that will give the protection which I think is needed against abuse and yet that will enable the legitimate case to get the benefit of the section.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
May I
make one suggestion to the minister? I rather blush to make it because I have often talked in the house against discretion. But in order to get the benefit of this provision and to give it a fair start and until perhaps a more detailed protection against breach can be found, would not the minister consider using words to indicate that the minister shall have a discretion in those cases in which it is perfectly clear that an invasion of the act is intended? I do not think it would be difficult. It seems to me that no large company would dare to break itself up if it knew it had to face this test. With regard to small companies and new corporations, surely common sense would decide the thing. Where there is actually a separate enterprise that surely is the test.

Income Tax Act
Surely it is not really a test of shareholding; it is a test really whether there is a separate enterprise which is going to aid production in this country. I think that is what the minister had in mind when he made his speech last March. It seems to me it would be a great pity if his proposal is to be almost still-born by being hedged about in this way. Incidentally I think the section is going to be very difficult to administer. I do suggest to the minister that the loss to the treasury is going to be trivial. How many of these can you imagine taking place in the next few months? If you let your imagination run it could extend perhaps to say only a few hundred. The difference that you would lose as between the 10 per cent and the 33 per cent would be $2,300 a company. So if you had a thousand of them it would only be $2 million. It does seem to me-

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What is $2 million?

speechtext: I am using an outside figure. I do not believe there would be a thousand, I do not believe there would be a hundred. I am giving the minister an outside figure to show what I think it is.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend. I will give consideration to every possibility here and I hope I shall be able to find a satisfactory solution. A number of suggestions have been made. As I say, I have not been able to convince myself yet that any one of them is the proper one. I have found from experience in these matters that unless you get something that is logical and sound in principle you get yourself into more trouble than you cure. Therefore I hope the committee will accept my assurance that between now and the time we have to look at this act again in the next few months I shall consider every alternative and see if I can improve the section, and of course any improvement will be made effective to the first period to which it applied, namely, the 1949 period.

IMr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
hardship on them. There are a number of comparatively small mines there which are subsidiaries of or related to other companies, or the stock is held by another coal mining company. subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Saskatchewan PREMIER'S OFFICE
Regina, November 29, 1949
Hon. Douglas C. Abbott,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Abbott:
Re rent control
Thank you for your letter of the twenty-third instant stating that the federal government is willing to amend orders 813 and 814, which provide for the recent rent increases, so that they will be inoperative in Saskatchewan. The Saskatchewan government is pleased to know that the federal government is prepared to co-operate with us to this extent. However, you will remember that our proposals were contingent on adequate assurance being received that our legislation will not be declared invalid by the Supreme Court of Canada. You stated, "I am advised that there is no reasonable doubt regarding this point and that a reference to the supreme court is unnecessary."
With due respect, as there is a difference of opinion as to reasonable doubt, we would again request that the question be submitted to the supreme court for a ruling. This point should be made absolutely clear in order to safeguard the interests of both the landlord and tenant. As the question of jurisdiction is already being referred to the supreme court, there seems little reason why a second reference should not be made.
If it is decided by the supreme court that the federal government has jurisdiction at the present time, it does not necessarily follow that by rescinding your power in regard to one province, the legislation that province enacts will be valid.
Frankly, my government cannot understand your reluctance to obtain a ruling. No constitutional lawyer can be certain on a point of this kind, which has never received judicial consideration. Landlords and tenants are entitled to every reasonable guarantee that can be given them that any provincial legislation that is passed will be valid. You are in a position to get that guarantee for them without much extra work or extra cost.
Again, with respect, in spite of your decided opinion that our legislation will be jurisdictionally valid, we must remind you of the fact that your law officers were of the opinion that the federal government has jurisdiction in the rent control field at the present time. This opinion did not, however, preclude you from making a reference of the question to the supreme court. At the time of that reference you stated:
"May I say at this point that the advice which the government receives from its law officers is that the existing federal regulations with respect to rent control are valid. But in a matter which concerns the welfare of so many Canadians, the government would not be discharging its responsibility to the people of Canada as it should if it did not take every precaution. It is possible that the courts would decide that our regulations are unconstitutional. We cannot disregard that possibility".
There you have stated your case frankly and, we think, correctly. You will note that that is also
our position. The government of Saskatchewan asks that on behalf of the welfare of the people of this province the "possibility" of a ruling by the supreme court contrary to you and your law officers' decided opinion cannot be disregarded.
With these doubts in mind, we therefore request that a second such reference be made to the supreme court. If your advisers are so certain of the outcome, the reference should be expeditiously dealt with.
Yours sincerely,
T. C. Douglas

My dear Premier:
Thank you for your letter of November 29, which I received a day or so ago.
As stated in my letter to you of November 23, the federal government agreed to suspend the recent changes in the rentals regulations as they apply in Saskatchewan, only on the condition that the Saskatchewan government gave a firm undertaking that it intended to introduce its own legislation not later than April 1, 1950, and requested the federal government to withdraw its rental regulations as from the same date.
The purpose of this arrangement was to create a position similar to what it would have been had your province acted at an earlier date and been ready to put its legislation into effect now. Otherwise, of course, we should not be justified in imposing more regid restrictions on home owners in Saskatchewan than we believe is proper and right in Canada generally, having in mind the purpose for which rental controls were imposed and the fact that virtually all other wartime controls have been removed. The entire arrangement depends upon your willingness to accept responsibility for the withdrawal of federal controls in Saskatchewan as from April 1, 1950. We cannot advise you as to the wisdom of such a step. Our position is simply that we are willing to withdraw the federal regulations in Saskatchewan so that there can then be no conflict between federal and provincial laws.
My colleagues and I have been giving further consideration to your request that another question be referred to the supreme court, relating to the validity of provincial legislation that may be operative after the federal government has removed its rentals regulations in that province. As you may have noticed from the press, our counsel notified the chief justice of the supreme court that it was possible that the reference might be amended as a result of correspondence that was taking place between the government of Canada and the government of Saskatchewan.
After a most careful review we are confirmed in our opinion that it is both unnecessary and undesirable to refer such a question to the supreme court. The validity of existing federal rent controls has been challenged in the courts, and we believe that we have a responsibility to the people of Canada to put the matter to a conclusive test with the least possible delay. Mr. Minister of Finance:
I received today your answer by wire to the [DOT]telegram which I sent you yesterday and in which I informed you that I had not received the federal orders in council relating to federal rental control.
We have noted your telegram to the effect that there is at present in this matter only one federal order in council in force, namely No. 9029 dated November 21, 1941.
These two telegrams and your letter dated November 24, delivered at my office Saturday the 26th and communicated to me Monday the 28th, were submitted to my colleagues of the executive council at a first meeting, held today.
You said you would comment on only one or two of the many points raised in the letter I had written to you recently. You state that the federal government's offer respecting rent control was unconditional and without any qualification whatever. Then you added: "I therefore find it difficult to understand the statement in your letter of November 16, 1949".
Apparently my statement was misunderstood. However, the facts show that it was correct.
On October £3, 1948 you wrote to me this:
"The constitutionality of continuing federal rent control has already been questioned and is now before the courts."
And you added:
"The federal government does not wish to do anything to prevent any province from making provisions to deal with the situation that would arise should continuing federal rent control be held invalid."
I have underlined the word "should" to stress the conditional character of your proposal.
Then, in your letter of November 9 you say: "The government has therefore decided to refer the question of the validity of the rental regulations to the supreme court, in the hope and expectation that a decision will be given before the present legislation expires. As I have said, the law officers of the crown are of opinion that the rentals regulations are valid. They are also of opinion that both the law and the facts support the view that it lies within the authority of parliament to extend these regulations for a further period. Counsel will be instructed by the Attorney General of Canada to press this view before the court."
It is clear that the federal authorities continue to claim a right to set up federal rental control,
and this attitude of theirs constitutes an obstacle to the full exercise of the rights of the provinces in the matter.
Brilliant lawyer that you are, you should not be unaware that it is contrary to sound tradition and to the best precedents to anticipate a judgment of the court to which the question has been referred. Nevertheless, eight years after entering a field which we consider exclusively provincial, you refer to the supreme court the question of the constitutionality of your rental control and at the same time you anticipate the decision of the supreme court, thus complicating the matter still further.
You pretend to offer the provinces the power to set up rent control. Therefore you persist in asserting that you possess such a right, and you place the province in the position of acknowledging a right of which we do not recognize the validity.
You will admit that the existence of two controls, one federal and one provincial, would be likely to aggravate the problem and, if possible, to increase its harmful consequences. This is indeed what would happen should Ottawa persist in its attitude, and if we did set up provincial control in the present circumstances.
For the past few years, as the federal authorities well know, and as you admitted in your letter of October 23, 1948, as well as in your previous letters, the constitutionality of federal rent control has been seriously questioned: nevertheless you continue to exercise powers which complicate the situation gravely while stating your desire to have the question of constitutionality decided by the supreme court.
The fact that you persist in claiming that rent control is a federal matter and that you have decided to maintain this viewpoint before the supreme court; the fact that you state in your letter that the federal government's law officers are of opinion that your rent control is constitutional-all that produces a situation which has to be taken into account and raises further and grave problems which do not tend to facilitate the settlement to be desired, and which we desire, of the difficulties caused and intensified by federal organizations.
It is easy to foresee the deplorable and complicated situation which would result from provincial control when the federal government continues to lay claim to the rights in question and asks the supreme court to sanction them.
It seems to us that the federal authority should not have constantly done and continue to do things of which the constitutionality is seriously questioned and is being submitted to the decision of the courts.
In claiming, as it does, the right to set up and to maintain rent control, the federal government asserts the right to set up at any time a federal control in opposition to provincial control.
The unfortunate victims of the federal decisions in this matter already have enough to complain of without their troubles and annoyances being aggravated by complications raised by the existence of both federal and provincial control.
You cite the example of the Saskatchewan government, which is apparently ready to set up provincial rental control. That is a matter which concerns the government of Saskatchewan. We have a clear mandate to administer the affairs of the province of Quebec, not of the province of Saskatchewan. Moreover, conditions vary from province to province and, that is one of the reasons why the rights of the provinces in this matter should have been respected at all times.
In short, we reaffirm that far from offering to the province the full exercise of its rights in this field, the federal government continues to render the full exercise thereof practically impossible.

We respectfully suggest to the federal government that it should modify its attitude and make it consistent with the rights of the provinces and with the rights of the people concerned. By removing, as you could easily do, the further and grave difficulties which you have added to the difficulties inherent in the problem, you would help solve the question rather than make it more complicated and more difficult. As to the present government of the province of Quebec, it is always ready to assume its responsibilities, but it desires that the federal government assume its own without any further delay.
Yours sincerely,
M. L. Duplessis
